```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.dates as mdates

# Load data
df = pd.read_csv("data.csv")
df["month"] = pd.to_datetime(df["month"], format="%Y-%m")
df = df.sort_values(["plan", "month"])

plans = ["Single", "Couple", "Family", "Vegetarian"]
colors = {
    "Single": "#1f77b4",
    "Couple": "#ff7f0e",
    "Family": "#d62728",
    "Vegetarian": "#2ca02c",
}

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(
    2, 1, figsize=(10, 6), sharex=True, gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [1.1, 1]}
)

for plan in plans:
    d = df[df["plan"] == plan]
    lw = 2.4 if plan == "Family" else 1.6
    ax1.plot(
        d["month"],
        d["active_subscribers"],
        marker="o",
        markersize=3.5,
        linewidth=lw,
        color=colors[plan],
        label=plan,
    )
    ax2.plot(
        d["month"],
        d["cancellation_rate_pct"],
        marker="o",
        markersize=3.5,
        linewidth=lw,
        color=colors[plan],
        label=plan,
    )

    ax.axvspan(sep_start, oct_start, color="0.85", alpha=0.35, zorder=0)

ax1.set_title("Active subscribers and cancellation rates by plan")

    price_change,
    ax1.get_ylim()[1] * 0.96,
    " Family price\n $79→$89",
    va="top",
    ha="left",
    fontsize=8,
)

ax2.set_ylabel("Cancellation rate (%)")
ax2.set_xlabel("Month")
ax2.legend(loc="upper left", ncol=4, fontsize=8, frameon=False)
ax2.text(
    sep_start,
    ax2.get_ylim()[1] * 0.96,
    " Sep 2026\n partial",
    va="top",
    ha="left",
    fontsize=8,
    color="0.35",
)

ax2.xaxis.set_major_locator(mdates.MonthLocator(interval=2))
ax2.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%b %Y"))
plt.setp(ax2.get_xticklabels(), rotation=45, ha="right")

fig.tight_layout()
```

The chart shows the main story in the notes: Family plan cancellations roughly doubled after the April price rise, and the plan started shrinking while the other three kept growing.

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.dates as mdates

df = pd.read_csv("data.csv")
df["date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["month"] + "-01")

plans = ["Couple", "Family", "Single", "Vegetarian"]
FAMILY = "#c8423b"
GREYS = {"Couple": "#7a7a7a", "Single": "#a9a9a9", "Vegetarian": "#8f9aa3"}
price_change = pd.Timestamp("2026-04-01")

def color(p):
    return FAMILY if p == "Family" else GREYS[p]

def dodge(values, min_gap):
    """Spread label y-positions apart so they don't overlap."""
    order = np.argsort(values)
    pos = np.array(values, dtype=float)
    adj = pos.copy()
    for i in range(1, len(order)):
        prev, cur = order[i - 1], order[i]
        if adj[cur] - adj[prev] < min_gap:
            adj[cur] = adj[prev] + min_gap
    return adj

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(
    1, 2, figsize=(10, 6), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.15, 1]}
)

# Panel 1: cancellation rate. September is left out because it covers only 1-14 Sept.
full = df[df["month"] <= "2026-08"]

for p in plans:
    d = full[full["plan"] == p].sort_values("date")
    ax1.plot(d["date"], d["cancellation_rate_pct"], color=color(p),
             lw=2.6 if p == "Family" else 1.6, zorder=3 if p == "Family" else 2)

last1 = full[full["month"] == "2026-08"].set_index("plan")["cancellation_rate_pct"]
ys = dodge([last1[p] for p in plans], 0.32)
for p, y in zip(plans, ys):
    ax1.text(pd.Timestamp("2026-08-12"), y, p, color=color(p), va="center",
             fontsize=9.5, fontweight="bold" if p == "Family" else "normal")

ax1.axvline(price_change, color=FAMILY, ls="--", lw=1, alpha=0.7)
ax1.text(price_change + pd.Timedelta(days=4), 7.35,
         "Family price\n$79 → $89/week", color=FAMILY, fontsize=9, va="top")

fam = full[full["plan"] == "Family"]
pre = fam[fam["date"] < price_change]["cancellation_rate_pct"].mean()
post = fam[fam["date"] >= price_change]["cancellation_rate_pct"].mean()
ax1.text(pd.Timestamp("2025-12-20"), pre + 0.45, f"avg {pre:.1f}%",
         color=FAMILY, fontsize=9, ha="center")
ax1.text(pd.Timestamp("2026-06-01"), post - 0.75, f"avg {post:.1f}%",
         color=FAMILY, fontsize=9, ha="center")

ax1.set_ylim(0, 7.5)
ax1.set_xlim(pd.Timestamp("2025-09-20"), pd.Timestamp("2026-10-10"))
ax1.set_ylabel("Cancellations as % of active subscribers")
ax1.set_title("Monthly cancellation rate (Oct 2025 – Aug 2026)", fontsize=11, loc="left")

# Panel 2: active subscribers at start of month (the September start count is complete)
for p in plans:
    d = df[df["plan"] == p].sort_values("date")
    ax2.plot(d["date"], d["active_subscribers"] / 1000, color=color(p),
             lw=2.6 if p == "Family" else 1.6, zorder=3 if p == "Family" else 2)

last2 = df[df["month"] == "2026-09"].set_index("plan")["active_subscribers"] / 1000
ys2 = dodge([last2[p] for p in plans], 1.2)
for p, y in zip(plans, ys2):
    ax2.text(pd.Timestamp("2026-09-12"), y, f"{p} {last2[p]:.1f}k", color=color(p),
             va="center", fontsize=9.5, fontweight="bold" if p == "Family" else "normal")

ax2.axvline(price_change, color=FAMILY, ls="--", lw=1, alpha=0.7)
ax2.annotate("Family: −19%\nsince April", xy=(pd.Timestamp("2026-07-01"), 12.7),
             xytext=(pd.Timestamp("2026-04-20"), 9.0), color=FAMILY, fontsize=9,
             arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=FAMILY, lw=0.8))

ax2.set_ylim(0, 24)
ax2.set_xlim(pd.Timestamp("2025-09-20"), pd.Timestamp("2026-12-15"))
ax2.set_ylabel("Active subscribers (thousands)")
ax2.set_title("Active subscribers, start of month", fontsize=11, loc="left")

for ax in (ax1, ax2):
    ax.xaxis.set_major_locator(mdates.MonthLocator(bymonth=[10, 1, 4, 7]))
    ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%b\n%Y"))
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
    ax.grid(axis="y", color="#e6e6e6", lw=0.8)
    ax.set_axisbelow(True)
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=9)

fig.suptitle("Family plan cancellations doubled after the April price rise, "
             "and the plan began shrinking", fontsize=13, fontweight="bold",
             x=0.02, ha="left")
fig.text(0.02, 0.015,
         "September 2026 cancellation rate is omitted: that month's data covers 1–14 Sept only. "
         "Figures exclude gift subscriptions (about 3% of orders).",
         fontsize=8, color="#555555", ha="left")

fig.tight_layout(rect=[0, 0.04, 1, 0.95])
```

- **Left panel:** Monthly cancellation rate for each plan from October 2025 to August 2026. A dashed line marks the April price rise. Family's average went from 3.1% to 6.5% a month, while the other plans stayed between about 2.3% and 3.2%. I left out September's rate because that month only covers 1–14 September, so its lower figure would look like a recovery when it isn't.
- **Right panel:** Active subscribers at the start of each month, which is a complete count even for September. Family fell 19% from April, while Couple, Single and Vegetarian all grew.

Family is shown in red and the other plans in grey so the comparison stands out.

```python
)

).sort_index()
```

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.dates as mdates

df = pd.read_csv("data.csv")
df["date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["month"] + "-01")
df = df.sort_values(["plan", "date"])

FAM = "#c0392b"
GREY = "#b5b5b5"
rise_date = pd.Timestamp("2026-04-01")

fam = df[df["plan"] == "Family"].copy()
fam["weekly_rev_k"] = fam["active_subscribers"] * fam["price_per_week_usd"] / 1000

# September covers 1-14 Sep only, so leave it out of the monthly cancellation rate
full = df[df["month"] != "2026-09"]
fam_full = full[full["plan"] == "Family"]
pre_rate = fam_full.loc[fam_full["date"] < rise_date, "cancellation_rate_pct"].mean()
post_rate = fam_full.loc[fam_full["date"] >= rise_date, "cancellation_rate_pct"].mean()

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 6), gridspec_kw={"wspace": 0.28})

# Panel 1: monthly cancellation rate
for i, (plan, g) in enumerate(full[full["plan"] != "Family"].groupby("plan")):
    ax1.plot(g["date"], g["cancellation_rate_pct"], color=GREY, lw=1.5,
             label="Other plans" if i == 0 else None)
ax1.plot(fam_full["date"], fam_full["cancellation_rate_pct"], color=FAM, lw=3,
         marker="o", ms=4, label="Family")

ax1.set_ylim(0, 8)
ax1.set_title("Monthly cancellation rate (%)", loc="left", fontsize=12, fontweight="bold")
ax1.text(pd.Timestamp("2025-10-10"), pre_rate + 0.55,
         f"avg {pre_rate:.1f}% at $79", color=FAM, fontsize=10)
ax1.text(pd.Timestamp("2026-04-10"), post_rate + 0.55,
         f"avg {post_rate:.1f}% at $89", color=FAM, fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")
ax1.legend(loc="lower left", frameon=False, fontsize=9)

# Panel 2: Family weekly revenue
pre_level = fam.loc[fam["month"] == "2026-03", "weekly_rev_k"].iloc[0]
peak = fam.loc[fam["month"] == "2026-04", "weekly_rev_k"].iloc[0]
latest = fam.loc[fam["month"] == "2026-09", "weekly_rev_k"].iloc[0]

ax2.plot(fam["date"], fam["weekly_rev_k"], color=FAM, lw=3, marker="o", ms=4)
ax2.axhline(pre_level, color="#555555", ls="--", lw=1.2)
ax2.text(pd.Timestamp("2025-10-05"), pre_level + 12,
         f"March level at $79: ${pre_level/1000:.2f}M", fontsize=9, color="#555555")
ax2.annotate(f"${peak/1000:.2f}M", (pd.Timestamp("2026-04-01"), peak),
             xytext=(6, 6), textcoords="offset points", color=FAM, fontsize=10)
ax2.annotate(f"${latest/1000:.2f}M\n(Sep)", (pd.Timestamp("2026-09-01"), latest),
             xytext=(-10, -36), textcoords="offset points", color=FAM,
             fontsize=10, fontweight="bold", ha="center")
ax2.set_ylim(900, 1350)
ax2.set_title("Family weekly revenue ($ thousands)", loc="left", fontsize=12, fontweight="bold")

for ax in (ax1, ax2):
    ax.axvline(rise_date, color="#333333", lw=1, ls=":")
    ax.text(rise_date, ax.get_ylim()[1], " Price $79→$89", va="top", fontsize=9, color="#333333")

    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

fig.suptitle("Family price rise doubled cancellations; weekly revenue is now below its pre-rise level",
```

```python
import pandas as pd
```

```python
periods = ["Sep 14-25\n(before fix)", "Sep 26-27\n(after fix)"]
variants = ["control", "new_checkout"]
```

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.ticker import FuncFormatter
from matplotlib.patches import Patch

df = pd.read_csv("data.csv")

# Order departments by total forecast variance
dept_order = (
    df.groupby("department")["variance_k"]
    .sum()
    .sort_values(ascending=False)
    .index
    .tolist()
)

lines = ["Staff", "Overtime", "Contracts", "Materials", "Fleet"]
colors = {
    "Staff": "#4C72B0",
    "Overtime": "#DD8452",
    "Contracts": "#55A868",
    "Materials": "#C44E52",
    "Fleet": "#8172B3",
}

pivot = (
    df.pivot_table(
        index="department",
        columns="budget_line",
        values="variance_k",
        aggfunc="sum"
    )
    .reindex(dept_order)
)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
x = np.arange(len(dept_order))
pos_bottom = np.zeros(len(dept_order))
neg_bottom = np.zeros(len(dept_order))

for line in lines:
    vals = pivot[line].fillna(0).values
    pos = np.where(vals > 0, vals, 0)
    neg = np.where(vals < 0, vals, 0)

    ax.bar(
        x, pos, bottom=pos_bottom, color=colors[line],
        width=0.72, edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.6
    )
    ax.bar(
        x, neg, bottom=neg_bottom, color=colors[line],
        width=0.72, edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.6
    )

    pos_bottom += pos
    neg_bottom += neg

ax.axhline(0, color="black", linewidth=0.8)
ax.set_xticks(x)
ax.set_xticklabels(dept_order)
ax.set_ylabel("Forecast variance ($ millions)")
ax.set_title(
    "Forecast Year-End Budget Variance by Department and Budget Line\n"
    f"City total: {df['variance_k'].sum() / 1000:+.1f}M forecast overspend",
    fontsize=12,
)
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(FuncFormatter(lambda y, _: f"${y / 1000:.1f}M"))
ax.grid(axis="y", linestyle="--", alpha=0.35)
ax.set_axisbelow(True)
ax.margins(y=0.16)

# Add department total labels
totals = df.groupby("department")["variance_k"].sum()
for xi, dept in zip(x, dept_order):
    total = totals.loc[dept]
    ax.annotate(
        f"{total / 1000:+.1f}M",
        (xi, total),
        xytext=(0, 6 if total >= 0 else -12),
        textcoords="offset points",
        ha="center",
        va="bottom" if total >= 0 else "top",
        fontsize=9,
        fontweight="bold",
    )

# Highlight Transit overtime
transit_x = dept_order.index("Transit")
transit_ot = df.loc[
    (df["department"] == "Transit") & (df["budget_line"] == "Overtime"),
    "variance_k",
].iloc[0]
transit_staff = df.loc[
    (df["department"] == "Transit") & (df["budget_line"] == "Staff"),
    "variance_k",
].iloc[0]
ot_mid = max(transit_staff, 0) + transit_ot / 2

ax.annotate(
    "Transit overtime\n+$2.4M",
    xy=(transit_x + 0.36, ot_mid),
    xytext=(transit_x + 0.62, ot_mid + 900),
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", lw=0.8, color="gray"),
    fontsize=9,
    ha="left",
    va="center",
)

handles = [
    Patch(facecolor=colors[line], edgecolor="white", label=line)
    for line in lines
]
ax.legend(
    handles=handles,
    title="Budget line",
    loc="upper right",
    frameon=False,
    fontsize=9,
    title_fontsize=9,
)

plt.tight_layout()
```

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
```

```python
df = pd.read_csv("data.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
```

```python
    df.groupby(["device", "variant"], as_index=False)[["sessions", "orders"]]
    .sum()
)

conv = agg.pivot(index="device", columns="variant", values="conversion")

sessions_by_device = df.groupby("device")["sessions"].sum()
```

## Analyst notes
- Courier prices are within 50 cents of each other ($9.28 to $9.73 per delivery).
- Customer ratings are similar (4.2 to 4.3 out of 5).
- Cold packs keep these medicines safe for 48 hours. Swiftline delivered 14.4% of parcels after more than 48 hours, against 2.2% for Northway and 2.5% for ParcelPro.
- Each courier damaged one parcel.
- Rural deliveries take about 4 hours longer than urban and suburban ones.
- Swiftline is fastest on a typical delivery: a median of 17.9 hours, against 22.5 for Northway and 21.2 for ParcelPro.
- Parcels shipped on Mondays take longest, because of the weekend backlog.
- Overall, 17% of deliveries arrived after the time promised to the customer.
- ParcelPro only started in September, so its figures rest on 40 deliveries, against 90 for each of the others. Its single delivery over 48 hours could easily be two or three in a larger sample.
- Delivery time rises with distance (correlation 0.39 for deliveries under 48 hours).

## Task
Make a chart from this.

## Output
Write Python code that draws the chart with matplotlib. pandas and numpy are available; no other libraries.
- Read the data from the file data.csv in the working directory.
- Make one figure with figsize=(10, 6). It may contain more than one panel.
- Do not call plt.show() or savefig(); the figure is saved for you.
Reply with the code in a single ```python code block.

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = pd.read_csv("data.csv")
df["over48"] = df["actual_hours"] > 48

order = ["Swiftline", "Northway", "ParcelPro"]
LIMIT = 48
c_ok = "#9aa5b1"
c_bad = "#c0392b"

stats = (df.groupby("courier")
           .agg(n=("actual_hours", "size"),
                median=("actual_hours", "median"),
                over=("over48", "sum"))
           .reindex(order))
stats["pct"] = 100 * stats["over"] / stats["n"]

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(
    1, 2, figsize=(10, 6), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.6, 1]}
)

# Left panel: every delivery, with the 48-hour cold-pack limit
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
for i, c in enumerate(order):
    sub = df[df["courier"] == c]
    x = i + rng.uniform(-0.22, 0.22, len(sub))
    colors = np.where(sub["over48"], c_bad, c_ok)
    ax1.scatter(x, sub["actual_hours"], s=22, c=colors, alpha=0.8,
                edgecolors="white", linewidths=0.4, zorder=3)
    med = stats.loc[c, "median"]
    ax1.hlines(med, i - 0.3, i + 0.3, color="black", lw=2.2, zorder=4)
    ax1.text(i + 0.32, med, f"median\n{med:.1f} h", va="center",
             ha="left", fontsize=8.5)

ax1.axhline(LIMIT, color=c_bad, ls="--", lw=1.3, zorder=2)
ax1.text(-0.45, LIMIT + 1.2, "48 h: cold packs stop protecting the medicine",
         color=c_bad, fontsize=9, va="bottom")
ax1.set_xticks(range(len(order)))
ax1.set_xticklabels([f"{c}\n(n={stats.loc[c, 'n']})" for c in order])
ax1.set_xlim(-0.5, len(order) - 0.5 + 0.35)
ax1.set_ylabel("Hours from dispatch to delivery")
ax1.set_ylim(0, max(80, df["actual_hours"].max() + 5))
ax1.set_title("Each dot is one delivery", fontsize=11, loc="left")
for s in ["top", "right"]:
    ax1.spines[s].set_visible(False)
ax1.grid(axis="y", alpha=0.3, zorder=0)

# Right panel: share of parcels over 48 hours
y = np.arange(len(order))[::-1]
bar_colors = [c_bad if c == "Swiftline" else c_ok for c in order]
ax2.barh(y, stats["pct"], color=bar_colors, height=0.55, zorder=3)
for yi, c in zip(y, order):
    p = stats.loc[c, "pct"]
    ax2.text(p + 0.4, yi, f"{p:.1f}%  ({int(stats.loc[c, 'over'])} of {stats.loc[c, 'n']})",
             va="center", fontsize=10)
ax2.set_yticks(y)
ax2.set_yticklabels(order)
ax2.set_xlim(0, max(stats["pct"]) * 1.6)
ax2.set_xlabel("% of parcels delivered after more than 48 h")
ax2.set_title("Parcels past the cold-pack limit", fontsize=11, loc="left")
for s in ["top", "right"]:
    ax2.spines[s].set_visible(False)
ax2.grid(axis="x", alpha=0.3, zorder=0)

fig.suptitle("Swiftline is fastest on a typical delivery, but about 1 in 7 of its "
             "parcels\narrive after the 48-hour cold-pack limit",
             fontsize=13, fontweight="bold", x=0.02, ha="left")
fig.text(0.02, 0.015,
         "Aug–Oct 2026. Prices ($9.28–$9.73 per delivery) and customer ratings (4.2–4.3 of 5) "
         "are similar across couriers.\nParcelPro started in September, so its rate rests on "
         "only 40 deliveries; one late parcel more or less moves it by 2.5 points.",
         fontsize=8.5, color="#555555", ha="left", va="bottom")

fig.tight_layout(rect=[0, 0.08, 1, 0.9])
```

## Output
Write Python code that draws the chart with matplotlib. pandas and numpy are available; no other libraries.
- Read the data from the file data.csv in the working directory.

```python
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = pd.read_csv("data.csv")

# Forecast variance by department, in $ millions (positive = overspend)
dept = df.groupby("department")["variance_k"].sum().div(1000).sort_values(ascending=False)
total = dept.sum()

transit_total = dept["Transit"]
transit_ot = df.query("department == 'Transit' and budget_line == 'Overtime'")["variance_k"].iloc[0] / 1000
transit_ot_pct = df.query("department == 'Transit' and budget_line == 'Overtime'")["variance_pct"].iloc[0]
transit_other = transit_total - transit_ot
roads = dept["Roads"]
roads_risk = 1.5
share = transit_total / total * 100

STRONG = "#C0392B"
STRONG_LIGHT = "#E8A79F"
GREY = "#BDBDBD"
DARK_GREY = "#7F7F7F"
TEXT = "#333333"

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.11, right=0.97, top=0.80, bottom=0.12)

names = list(dept.index)
y = range(len(names))
h = 0.68

for i, name in enumerate(names):
    v = dept[name]
    if name == "Transit":
        ax.barh(i, transit_ot, height=h, color=STRONG, zorder=3)
        ax.barh(i, transit_other, left=transit_ot, height=h, color=STRONG_LIGHT, zorder=3)
    elif name == "Roads":
        ax.barh(i, v, height=h, color=DARK_GREY, zorder=3)
    else:
        ax.barh(i, v, height=h, color=GREY, zorder=3)

ti = names.index("Transit")
ri = names.index("Roads")
pi = names.index("Police")

# Transit annotations
ax.text(transit_ot / 2, ti, f"Overtime +${transit_ot:.1f}M", ha="center", va="center",
        color="white", fontsize=10.5, fontweight="bold", zorder=4)
ax.text(transit_total + 0.08, ti - 0.13, f"+${transit_total:.1f}M  ({share:.0f}% of city total)",
        ha="left", va="center", color=STRONG, fontsize=12, fontweight="bold")
ax.text(transit_total + 0.08, ti + 0.25,
        f"Overtime is {transit_ot_pct:.0f}% over its ${2.0:.1f}M budget:\ndriver vacancies covered by extra shifts",
        ha="left", va="top", color=TEXT, fontsize=9.5)

# Roads: harsh-winter risk shown as hatched extension
ax.barh(ri, roads_risk, left=roads, height=h, facecolor="none", edgecolor=DARK_GREY,
        hatch="///", linewidth=0.8, linestyle="--", zorder=3)
ax.text(roads / 2, ri, f"+${roads:.1f}M", ha="center", va="center",
        color="white", fontsize=10, fontweight="bold", zorder=4)
ax.text(roads + roads_risk + 0.08, ri,
        f"Harsh winter could add up to ${roads_risk:.1f}M\n(forecast assumes average snow clearing)\n"
        f"→ ${roads + roads_risk:.1f}M, still below Transit",
        ha="left", va="center", color=TEXT, fontsize=9.5)

# Police label
ax.text(dept["Police"] + 0.06, pi, f"+${dept['Police']:.1f}M", ha="left", va="center",
        color=TEXT, fontsize=10)

# Axes styling
ax.set_yticks(list(y))
ax.set_yticklabels(names, fontsize=10.5, color=TEXT)
ax.get_yticklabels()[ti].set_color(STRONG)
ax.get_yticklabels()[ti].set_fontweight("bold")
ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.axvline(0, color=TEXT, linewidth=0.9, zorder=4)
ax.set_xlim(-0.6, 6.0)
ax.set_xticks([-0.5, 0, 1, 2, 3])
ax.set_xticklabels(["−$0.5M", "$0", "$1M", "$2M", "$3M"], fontsize=9.5, color=TEXT)
ax.set_xlabel("Forecast year-end spending minus approved budget ($ millions; right of zero = overspend)",
              fontsize=9.5, color=TEXT)
ax.grid(axis="x", color="#EEEEEE", zorder=0)
for s in ["top", "right", "left"]:
    ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["bottom"].set_color("#999999")
ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=0)

# Title and subtitle
fig.text(0.02, 0.95, f"Transit drives {share:.0f}% of the city's ${total:.1f}M forecast overspend — review Transit",
         fontsize=15, fontweight="bold", color=TEXT, ha="left")
fig.text(0.02, 0.895,
         f"Forecast overspend by department, City of Marlow, full year. City total: +${total:.1f}M. "
         f"Next largest: Roads +${roads:.1f}M, Police +${dept['Police']:.1f}M.",
         fontsize=10.5, color="#555555", ha="left")
```

## Analyst notes
- Courier prices are within 50 cents of each other ($9.28 to $9.73 per delivery).
- Customer ratings are similar (4.2 to 4.3 out of 5).
- Cold packs keep these medicines safe for 48 hours. Swiftline delivered 14.4% of parcels after more than 48 hours, against 2.2% for Northway and 2.5% for ParcelPro.
- Each courier damaged one parcel.
- Rural deliveries take about 4 hours longer than urban and suburban ones.
- Swiftline is fastest on a typical delivery: a median of 17.9 hours, against 22.5 for Northway and 21.2 for ParcelPro.
- Parcels shipped on Mondays take longest, because of the weekend backlog.
- Overall, 17% of deliveries arrived after the time promised to the customer.
- ParcelPro only started in September, so its figures rest on 40 deliveries, against 90 for each of the others. Its single delivery over 48 hours could easily be two or three in a larger sample.
- Delivery time rises with distance (correlation 0.39 for deliveries under 48 hours).

## Output
Write Python code that draws the chart with matplotlib. pandas and numpy are available; no other libraries.
- Read the data from the file data.csv in the working directory.

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = pd.read_csv("data.csv")

couriers = ["Swiftline", "Northway", "ParcelPro"]
colors = {"Swiftline": "#1f77b4", "Northway": "#ff7f0e", "ParcelPro": "#2ca02c"}

# Courier-level summary: sample size, share over 48h, and Wilson 95% CI
summary = []
for c in couriers:
    vals = df.loc[df["courier"] == c, "actual_hours"].dropna()
    n = len(vals)
    k = int((vals > 48).sum())
    p = k / n
    z = 1.96
    denom = 1 + z * z / n
    center = (p + z * z / (2 * n)) / denom
    half = z * np.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n + z * z / (4 * n * n)) / denom
    summary.append({
        "courier": c,
        "n": n,
        "pct": p * 100,
        "ci_low": max(0, (center - half) * 100),
        "ci_high": min(100, (center + half) * 100),
    })

summary = pd.DataFrame(summary)

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(
    1, 2, figsize=(10, 6), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.1, 1]}
)

# Left panel: ECDF of actual delivery time
for c in couriers:
    vals = np.sort(df.loc[df["courier"] == c, "actual_hours"].dropna().values)
    n = len(vals)
    y = np.arange(1, n + 1) / n * 100
    ax1.step(
        vals, y, where="post", color=colors[c], linewidth=2.2,
        label=f"{c} (n={n})"
    )

ax1.axvline(48, color="crimson", linestyle="--", linewidth=1.4)
ax1.text(48.8, 8, "48 h cold-pack limit", color="crimson", fontsize=9, va="bottom")
ax1.set_xlabel("Actual delivery time (hours)")
ax1.set_ylabel("Cumulative share of deliveries (%)")
ax1.set_title("Delivery time distributions")
ax1.set_xlim(0, df["actual_hours"].max() + 5)
ax1.set_ylim(0, 100)
ax1.grid(axis="y", alpha=0.25)
ax1.legend(frameon=False, loc="lower right")

# Right panel: percentage over 48h with 95% confidence intervals
x = np.arange(len(summary))
bar_colors = [colors[c] for c in summary["courier"]]
ax2.bar(x, summary["pct"], color=bar_colors, width=0.6, edgecolor="none")

yerr_low = summary["pct"] - summary["ci_low"]
yerr_high = summary["ci_high"] - summary["pct"]
ax2.errorbar(
    x, summary["pct"], yerr=[yerr_low, yerr_high],
    fmt="none", ecolor="black", capsize=5, linewidth=1.1
)

for i, row in summary.iterrows():
    ax2.text(
        i, row["ci_high"] + 0.8, f"{row['pct']:.1f}%",
        ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=10, fontweight="bold"
    )

ax2.set_xticks(x)
ax2.set_xticklabels(
    [f"{row['courier']}\n(n={int(row['n'])})" for _, row in summary.iterrows()]
)
ax2.set_ylabel("Deliveries over 48 hours (%)")
ax2.set_title("Cold-chain risk by courier (95% CI)")
ax2.set_ylim(0, max(summary["ci_high"]) + 5)
ax2.grid(axis="y", alpha=0.25)

fig.suptitle(
    "Courier performance: typical speed and long-delivery risk",
    fontsize=14, fontweight="bold"
)
plt.tight_layout(rect=[0, 0, 1, 0.95])
```

## Analyst notes
- Courier prices are within 50 cents of each other ($9.28 to $9.73 per delivery).
- Customer ratings are similar (4.2 to 4.3 out of 5).
- Cold packs keep these medicines safe for 48 hours. Swiftline delivered 14.4% of parcels after more than 48 hours, against 2.2% for Northway and 2.5% for ParcelPro.
- Each courier damaged one parcel.
- Rural deliveries take about 4 hours longer than urban and suburban ones.
- Swiftline is fastest on a typical delivery: a median of 17.9 hours, against 22.5 for Northway and 21.2 for ParcelPro.
- Parcels shipped on Mondays take longest, because of the weekend backlog.
- Overall, 17% of deliveries arrived after the time promised to the customer.
- ParcelPro only started in September, so its figures rest on 40 deliveries, against 90 for each of the others. Its single delivery over 48 hours could easily be two or three in a larger sample.
- Delivery time rises with distance (correlation 0.39 for deliveries under 48 hours).

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = pd.read_csv("data.csv")
df["late"] = df["late"].astype(str).str.lower().eq("true")

LIMIT = 48
couriers = ["Swiftline", "Northway", "ParcelPro"]
ypos = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(reversed(couriers))}  # Swiftline at top

def wilson(k, n, z=1.96):
    p = k / n
    denom = 1 + z**2 / n
    centre = (p + z**2 / (2 * n)) / denom
    half = z * np.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n + z**2 / (4 * n**2)) / denom
    return p, max(0, centre - half), centre + half

stats = {}
for c in couriers:
    d = df[df["courier"] == c]
    k = int((d["actual_hours"] > LIMIT).sum())
    n = len(d)
    p, lo, hi = wilson(k, n)
    stats[c] = dict(k=k, n=n, p=p, lo=lo, hi=hi,
                    median=d["actual_hours"].median(),
                    cost=d["cost_usd"].mean())

RED = "#c0392b"
GREY = "#8c8c8c"
DARK = "#2b2b2b"

)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.12, right=0.97, top=0.78, bottom=0.14)

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)

for c in couriers:
    d = df[df["courier"] == c]
    y = ypos[c] + rng.uniform(-0.22, 0.22, len(d))
    over = d["actual_hours"] > LIMIT
    ax1.scatter(d.loc[~over, "actual_hours"], y[~over.values], s=16,
                color=GREY, alpha=0.55, edgecolor="none", zorder=2)
    ax1.scatter(d.loc[over, "actual_hours"], y[over.values], s=30,
                color=RED, alpha=0.9, edgecolor="white", lw=0.5, zorder=3)
    m = stats[c]["median"]
    ax1.plot([m, m], [ypos[c] - 0.3, ypos[c] + 0.3], color=DARK, lw=2.2, zorder=4)
    ax1.text(m, ypos[c] + 0.33, f"median {m:.0f} h", ha="center", va="bottom",
             fontsize=8.5, color=DARK)

ax1.set_xlim(0, xmax)
ax1.set_ylim(-0.6, 2.6)
ax1.set_yticks([ypos[c] for c in couriers])
```

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = pd.read_csv("data.csv")

# Department totals, ordered by net forecast variance (largest overspend first)
dept = (
    df.groupby("department")
      .agg(budget_k=("annual_budget_k", "sum"), variance_k=("variance_k", "sum"))
      .sort_values("variance_k", ascending=False)
)
dept["variance_pct_total"] = 100 * dept["variance_k"] / dept["budget_k"]
order = list(dept.index)

# Variance by budget line, in $ million
lines = ["Staff", "Overtime", "Contracts", "Materials", "Fleet"]
pivot = (
    df.pivot_table(index="department", columns="budget_line",
                   values="variance_k", aggfunc="sum")
      .reindex(index=order, columns=lines)
      .fillna(0) / 1000.0
)

city_budget_m = dept["budget_k"].sum() / 1000.0
city_var_m = dept["variance_k"].sum() / 1000.0
city_pct = 100 * city_var_m / city_budget_m
transit_var_m = dept.loc["Transit", "variance_k"] / 1000.0
transit_share = 100 * transit_var_m / city_var_m
transit_ot = df.loc[
    (df["department"] == "Transit") & (df["budget_line"] == "Overtime")
].iloc[0]
transit_ot_var_m = transit_ot["variance_k"] / 1000.0
transit_ot_budget_m = transit_ot["annual_budget_k"] / 1000.0
transit_ot_pct = transit_ot["variance_pct"]

    "Staff": "#4C78A8",
    "Overtime": "#E45756",
    "Contracts": "#54A24B",
    "Materials": "#F58518",
    "Fleet": "#B279A2",
}

    1, 2, figsize=(10, 6), sharey=True,
    gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [3.0, 1.3], "wspace": 0.08},
)

y = np.arange(len(order))
pos_end = {}
net_m = dept["variance_k"].values / 1000.0

# Left panel: diverging stacked variance in $m
for i, dept_name in enumerate(order):
    pos, neg = 0.0, 0.0
    for line in lines:
        val = pivot.loc[dept_name, line]
        label = line if i == 0 else None
        if val >= 0:
            ax1.barh(i, val, left=pos, height=0.62,
                     color=colors[line], label=label)
            pos += val
        else:
            ax1.barh(i, abs(val), left=neg + val, height=0.62,
                     color=colors[line], label=label)
            neg += val
    pos_end[dept_name] = pos

# Roads harsh-winter scenario: not part of the forecast variance
roads_y = order.index("Roads")
ax1.barh(roads_y, 1.5, left=pos_end["Roads"], height=0.62,
         facecolor="none", edgecolor="#666666", hatch="///", linewidth=1.0)
ax1.annotate(

    xytext=(2.55, roads_y + 0.55),
    fontsize=8, color="#444444",
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color="#666666", lw=0.9),
)

# Net department variance markers and labels
ax1.plot(net_m, y, marker="D", color="black", markersize=5,
         linestyle="none", zorder=5, label="Department net")
for i, val in enumerate(net_m):
    offset = 0.10 if val >= 0 else -0.10
    ha = "left" if val >= 0 else "right"
    # Keep the Transit label clear of its long bar
    x_text = val + offset
    ax1.text(x_text, i - 0.32, f"{val:+.1f}", fontsize=8,
             ha=ha, va="center", fontweight="bold")

# Key annotation for the main driver
transit_y = order.index("Transit")
ax1.annotate(
    f"Transit overtime +${transit_ot_var_m:.1f}m\n"
    f"({transit_ot_pct:+.0f}% of its ${transit_ot_budget_m:.1f}m budget)",
    xy=(1.45, transit_y), xytext=(1.05, transit_y + 1.35),
    fontsize=8.5, fontweight="bold", color="#A52A2A",
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color="#A52A2A", lw=1.1),
)

ax1.axvline(0, color="black", linewidth=0.9)
ax1.set_xlim(-0.95, 4.15)
ax1.set_xlabel("Forecast variance, $ million\n(left = underspend, right = overspend)")
ax1.set_title("Where the overspend sits, by spending type ($m)", fontsize=11)
ax1.set_yticks(y)

    [f"{d} (${dept.loc[d, 'budget_k'] / 1000:.1f}m budget)" for d in order],
    fontsize=9,

ax1.invert_yaxis()
ax1.grid(axis="x", alpha=0.25)
ax1.set_axisbelow(True)
ax1.legend(loc="lower right", fontsize=8, framealpha=0.9, ncol=2)

# Right panel: variance relative to each department's own budget
pct = dept["variance_pct_total"].values
bar_colors = ["#C0392B" if v > 0 else "#2471A3" if v < 0 else "#7F8C8D"
```

## Task
Make a chart for the City of Marlow's finance committee, who must decide which department to put under a mid-year spending review. They will see it for about ten seconds on a slide in a meeting, so it should help them make that decision.

Design guidance:
- Pick the one message the audience most needs for this decision, and make the title state it as a sentence.
- Show only the data needed for that message. Leave out series, columns and notes that do not help the decision.
- Use one strong colour for what matters and grey for context. Label lines or bars directly instead of using a legend when you can.
- Add a number label only where the number is part of the message. Do not label every bar or point.
- If a caveat changes how the chart should be read, state it briefly on the chart.
- Keep scales honest: bar charts start at zero, units are labelled, no 3-D effects and no second y-axis.

## Output
Write Python code that draws the chart with matplotlib. pandas and numpy are available; no other libraries.
- Read the data from the file data.csv in the working directory.
- Make one figure with figsize=(10, 6). It may contain more than one panel.

```python
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = pd.read_csv("data.csv")

# Department totals only — the decision is which department to review.
dept_m = (df.groupby("department")["variance_k"].sum() / 1000).sort_values()
city_total_m = dept_m.sum()
transit_total_m = dept_m["Transit"]

ot = df[(df["department"] == "Transit") & (df["budget_line"] == "Overtime")].iloc[0]
transit_ot_m = ot["variance_k"] / 1000
transit_ot_pct = ot["variance_pct"]

GREY = "#B8B8B8"
RED = "#C1272D"
LIGHT_RED = "#E8A9AB"

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.13, right=0.96, top=0.80, bottom=0.18)

y = range(len(dept_m))
ax.barh(y, dept_m.values, color=GREY, height=0.62)

# Transit: total bar split to show its overtime driver (no legend needed).
ti = list(dept_m.index).index("Transit")
ax.barh(ti, transit_ot_m, color=RED, height=0.62)
ax.barh(ti, transit_total_m - transit_ot_m, left=transit_ot_m,
        color=LIGHT_RED, height=0.62)

ax.set_yticks(list(y))
ax.set_yticklabels(dept_m.index, fontsize=12)
for label in ax.get_yticklabels():
    if label.get_text() == "Transit":
        label.set_fontweight("bold")

ax.axvline(0, color="black", linewidth=1.2)
ax.set_xlim(-0.65, 3.85)
ax.set_xticks([-0.5, 0, 1, 2, 3])
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=11)
ax.set_xlabel("Forecast variance vs budget ($ million)  —  positive = overspend",
              fontsize=11)

ax.xaxis.grid(True, color="#E5E5E5", linewidth=0.8)
ax.set_axisbelow(True)
for spine in ["top", "right", "left"]:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)

# The one message, as the title.
ax.set_title(
    f"Put Transit under review: it accounts for ${transit_total_m:.1f}m of the\n"
    f"city's ${city_total_m:.1f}m forecast overspend (65%)",
    loc="left", fontsize=16, fontweight="bold", pad=26,
)
ax.text(0, 1.03, "Driver vacancies are being covered by extra shifts.",
        transform=ax.transAxes, fontsize=11.5, color="#444444")

# Number labels only where they carry the message.
ax.text(transit_ot_m / 2, ti, f"Overtime +${transit_ot_m:.1f}m\n(+{transit_ot_pct:.0f}%)",
        va="center", ha="center", fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", color="white")
ax.text(transit_total_m + 0.07, ti, f"${transit_total_m:.1f}m",
        va="center", ha="left", fontsize=13, fontweight="bold", color=RED)

fig.text(0.13, 0.045,
         "Department forecast year-end spending minus annual budget. Roads assumes average snow clearing; "
         "a harsh winter (+up to $1.5m)\nwould still leave Roads below Transit.",
         fontsize=8.5, color="#555555")
```

## Analyst notes
- Courier prices are within 50 cents of each other ($9.28 to $9.73 per delivery).
- Customer ratings are similar (4.2 to 4.3 out of 5).
- Cold packs keep these medicines safe for 48 hours. Swiftline delivered 14.4% of parcels after more than 48 hours, against 2.2% for Northway and 2.5% for ParcelPro.
- Each courier damaged one parcel.
- Rural deliveries take about 4 hours longer than urban and suburban ones.
- Swiftline is fastest on a typical delivery: a median of 17.9 hours, against 22.5 for Northway and 21.2 for ParcelPro.
- Parcels shipped on Mondays take longest, because of the weekend backlog.
- Overall, 17% of deliveries arrived after the time promised to the customer.
- ParcelPro only started in September, so its figures rest on 40 deliveries, against 90 for each of the others. Its single delivery over 48 hours could easily be two or three in a larger sample.
- Delivery time rises with distance (correlation 0.39 for deliveries under 48 hours).

## Task
Make a chart for Medley Pharmacy's operations director, who must decide which courier to contract for refrigerated medicine deliveries next year. They will see it for about ten seconds on a slide in a meeting, so it should help them make that decision.

Design guidance:
- Pick the one message the audience most needs for this decision, and make the title state it as a sentence.

- Add a number label only where the number is part of the message. Do not label every bar or point.

## Output
Write Python code that draws the chart with matplotlib. pandas and numpy are available; no other libraries.
- Read the data from the file data.csv in the working directory.
- Make one figure with figsize=(10, 6). It may contain more than one panel.

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = pd.read_csv("data.csv")
df["late"] = df["late"].astype(str).str.lower() == "true"

COLD_LIMIT = 48
order = ["Swiftline", "Northway", "ParcelPro"]

g = df.groupby("courier")
n = g.size().reindex(order)
over = g["actual_hours"].apply(lambda s: (s > COLD_LIMIT).sum()).reindex(order)
pct_over = 100 * over / n
median_h = g["actual_hours"].median().reindex(order)

STRONG = "#D1452B"
GREY = "#B8B8B8"
DARK = "#333333"

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(
    1, 2, figsize=(10, 6), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [3, 2], "wspace": 0.35}
)

y = np.arange(len(order))[::-1]  # Swiftline at top

# Left panel: share of parcels past the cold-pack limit (the decision metric)
colors1 = [STRONG if c == "Swiftline" else GREY for c in order]
ax1.barh(y, pct_over.values, color=colors1, height=0.6)
for yi, c in zip(y, order):
    label = f"{pct_over[c]:.1f}%  ({over[c]} of {n[c]})"
    ax1.text(pct_over[c] + 0.4, yi, label, va="center", fontsize=11,
             color=STRONG if c == "Swiftline" else DARK,
             fontweight="bold" if c == "Swiftline" else "normal")
ax1.set_yticks(y)
ax1.set_yticklabels(order, fontsize=12)
ax1.set_xlim(0, 22)
ax1.set_xlabel("% of parcels delivered after more than 48 hours", fontsize=10)
ax1.set_title("Parcels arriving after cold packs expire (>48 h)",
              fontsize=11, loc="left", color=DARK)

# Right panel: typical (median) delivery time, as context
ax2.barh(y, median_h.values, color=GREY, height=0.6)
for yi, c in zip(y, order):
    ax2.text(median_h[c] + 0.5, yi, f"{median_h[c]:.1f} h", va="center",
             fontsize=11, color=DARK)
ax2.set_yticks(y)
ax2.set_yticklabels(order, fontsize=12)
ax2.set_xlim(0, 30)
ax2.set_xlabel("Median delivery time, hours", fontsize=10)
ax2.set_title("Typical delivery time", fontsize=11, loc="left", color=DARK)

for ax in (ax1, ax2):
    for side in ("top", "right"):
        ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
    ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=0)
    ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=9, colors="#555555")

fig.suptitle(
    "Swiftline is fastest on a typical delivery, but 1 in 7 of its parcels\n"
    "arrived after the 48-hour cold packs had run out",
    fontsize=15, fontweight="bold", x=0.06, ha="left", y=0.98,
)

pp_one_more = 100 * (over["ParcelPro"] + 1) / n["ParcelPro"]
fig.text(
    0.06, 0.03,
    f"Caveat: ParcelPro started in September, so its rate rests on only {n['ParcelPro']} deliveries "
    f"(vs {n['Swiftline']} for the others).\nOne more slow parcel would raise it to {pp_one_more:.0f}%. "
    "Deliveries Aug–Oct 2026.",
    fontsize=9.5, color="#555555", ha="left", va="bottom",
)

fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.12, right=0.97, top=0.80, bottom=0.2)
```

## Analyst notes
- Courier prices are within 50 cents of each other ($9.28 to $9.73 per delivery).
- Customer ratings are similar (4.2 to 4.3 out of 5).
- Cold packs keep these medicines safe for 48 hours. Swiftline delivered 14.4% of parcels after more than 48 hours, against 2.2% for Northway and 2.5% for ParcelPro.
- Each courier damaged one parcel.
- Rural deliveries take about 4 hours longer than urban and suburban ones.
- Swiftline is fastest on a typical delivery: a median of 17.9 hours, against 22.5 for Northway and 21.2 for ParcelPro.
- Parcels shipped on Mondays take longest, because of the weekend backlog.
- Overall, 17% of deliveries arrived after the time promised to the customer.
- ParcelPro only started in September, so its figures rest on 40 deliveries, against 90 for each of the others. Its single delivery over 48 hours could easily be two or three in a larger sample.
- Delivery time rises with distance (correlation 0.39 for deliveries under 48 hours).

## Task
Make a chart for Medley Pharmacy's operations director, who must decide which courier to contract for refrigerated medicine deliveries next year. They will see it for about ten seconds on a slide in a meeting, so it should help them make that decision.

Design guidance:
- Pick the one message the audience most needs for this decision, and make the title state it as a sentence.
- Show only the data needed for that message. Leave out series, columns and notes that do not help the decision.
- Use one strong colour for what matters and grey for context. Label lines or bars directly instead of using a legend when you can.
- Add a number label only where the number is part of the message. Do not label every bar or point.
- If a caveat changes how the chart should be read, state it briefly on the chart.
- Keep scales honest: bar charts start at zero, units are labelled, no 3-D effects and no second y-axis.

## Output
Write Python code that draws the chart with matplotlib. pandas and numpy are available; no other libraries.
- Read the data from the file data.csv in the working directory.
- Make one figure with figsize=(10, 6). It may contain more than one panel.
- Do not call plt.show() or savefig(); the figure is saved for you.
Reply with the code in a single ```python code block.

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = pd.read_csv('data.csv')
df['actual_hours'] = pd.to_numeric(df['actual_hours'], errors='coerce')
df['over48'] = df['actual_hours'] > 48

summary = (
    df.groupby('courier')
      .agg(n=('actual_hours', 'size'), over48=('over48', 'sum'))
      .reset_index()
)
summary['pct_over48'] = summary['over48'] / summary['n'] * 100
summary = summary.sort_values('pct_over48', ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)

couriers = summary['courier'].tolist()
pct = summary['pct_over48'].to_numpy()
counts = summary['over48'].to_numpy()
ns = summary['n'].to_numpy()

colors = ['#C0392B' if c == 'Swiftline' else '#BDBDBD' for c in couriers]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
bars = ax.bar(couriers, pct, color=colors, width=0.62, edgecolor='none', zorder=3)

fig.suptitle(
    "For refrigerated medicines, choose Northway or ParcelPro: Swiftline breaches the 48-hour cold-chain limit far more often",
    x=0.02, y=0.98, ha='left', fontsize=13.8, fontweight='bold'
)
ax.set_title(
    "Share of deliveries taking more than 48 hours from dispatch to delivery, by courier",
    loc='left', fontsize=10.5, color='#555555', pad=12
)

ax.set_ylabel("% of deliveries over 48 hours", fontsize=11)
ymax = np.ceil(max(pct) * 1.35 / 2) * 2
ax.set_ylim(0, ymax)
ax.set_yticks(np.arange(0, ymax + 1, 2))
ax.set_yticklabels([f"{int(t)}%" for t in ax.get_yticks()])
ax.grid(axis='y', color='#E5E5E5', linewidth=0.8, zorder=0)
ax.set_axisbelow(True)

for spine in ['top', 'right']:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
ax.spines['left'].set_color('#999999')
ax.spines['bottom'].set_color('#999999')
ax.tick_params(axis='x', labelsize=12)
ax.tick_params(axis='y', labelsize=10, colors='#555555')

for bar, c, v, o, n in zip(bars, couriers, pct, counts, ns):
    highlight = (c == 'Swiftline')
    ax.text(
        bar.get_x() + bar.get_width() / 2,
        bar.get_height() + max(pct) * 0.035,
        f"{v:.1f}%\n({o} of {n})",
        ha='center', va='bottom',
        fontsize=11.5 if highlight else 10,
        color='#C0392B' if highlight else '#444444',
        fontweight='bold' if highlight else 'normal'
    )

fig.text(
    0.02, 0.02,
    "Cold packs keep these medicines safe for 48 hours.  ParcelPro is based on only 40 deliveries (1 over 48h), so its rate is less certain; Northway and Swiftline each have 90.",
    ha='left', va='bottom', fontsize=8.5, color='#555555'
)

plt.subplots_adjust(left=0.10, right=0.97, top=0.81, bottom=0.16)
```

## Analyst notes
- Large stores sit in bigger catchments: 85,000 to 140,000 people within 15 minutes, against 30,000 to 90,000 for standard stores.
- Large stores sell less per square foot: $469 a year on average, against $606 for standard stores.
- Parking spaces rise with floor area (correlation 0.96).
- The chain's top seller is S39 in Radley, a large store with $29.3 million in sales.
- A large store averages $21.8 million in annual sales against $15.0 million for a standard store: 46% more sales for 88% more floor space.
- Standard stores opened before 2010 sell about $19 more per square foot than newer standard stores.
- Staff numbers track sales closely, at about 6 employees per $1 million of sales in both formats.
- 4 of the 11 large stores opened in 2025 or 2026 and are still building up trade. Without them, large stores average $514 per square foot, still below standard stores.
- The average store has 29,950 square feet of selling space.
- Two stores closed for six weeks of renovation; their sales are annualised.

## Task
Make a chart from this.

## Output
Write Python code that draws the chart with matplotlib. pandas and numpy are available; no other libraries.
- Read the data from the file data.csv in the working directory.
- Make one figure with figsize=(10, 6). It may contain more than one panel.
- Do not call plt.show() or savefig(); the figure is saved for you.
Reply with the code in a single ```python code block.

```python
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.ticker import FuncFormatter

df = pd.read_csv("data.csv")

std = df[df["format"] == "standard"]
large = df[df["format"] == "large"]
large_new = large[large["opened_year"] >= 2025]
large_est = large[large["opened_year"] < 2025]

c_std = "#7f8c8d"
c_large = "#c0392b"

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))

ax.scatter(std["sq_ft"], std["sales_per_sqft_usd"], s=55, color=c_std, alpha=0.8,
           edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.6, label="Standard stores", zorder=3)
ax.scatter(large_est["sq_ft"], large_est["sales_per_sqft_usd"], s=70, color=c_large,
           edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.6, label="Large stores, opened before 2025", zorder=3)
ax.scatter(large_new["sq_ft"], large_new["sales_per_sqft_usd"], s=70, facecolor="white",
           edgecolor=c_large, linewidth=1.6,
           label="Large stores, opened 2025–26 (still building trade)", zorder=3)

# Group averages as short reference lines spanning each group's size range
def mean_line(sub, color, text, va="bottom"):
    m = sub["sales_per_sqft_usd"].mean()
    x0, x1 = sub["sq_ft"].min(), sub["sq_ft"].max()
    ax.hlines(m, x0, x1, colors=color, linestyles="--", linewidth=1.3, zorder=2)
    ax.text(x1 + 400, m, f"{text}: ${m:,.0f}", color=color, va="center",
            ha="left", fontsize=9.5)

mean_line(std, c_std, "Avg")
mean_line(large_est, c_large, "Avg")
mean_line(large_new, c_large, "Avg")

ax.set_xlabel("Selling floor area (sq ft)", fontsize=11)
ax.set_ylabel("Annual sales per square foot", fontsize=11)
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v/1000:,.0f}k"))
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"${v:,.0f}"))
ax.set_xlim(15000, 62000)
ax.set_ylim(330, 750)

for s in ["top", "right"]:
    ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
ax.grid(axis="y", color="#e5e5e5", linewidth=0.8, zorder=0)
ax.legend(loc="lower left", frameon=False, fontsize=9.5)

fig.suptitle("Large stores sell less per square foot than standard stores",
             x=0.06, ha="left", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold")
fig.text(0.06, 0.905,
         "Annual sales per sq ft by store size, 46 stores. The gap remains when the four "
         "large stores opened in 2025–26 are set aside.",
         ha="left", fontsize=10, color="#444444")

fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.1, right=0.97, top=0.86, bottom=0.1)
```

- Rural deliveries take about 4 hours longer than urban and suburban ones.
- Swiftline is fastest on a typical delivery: a median of 17.9 hours, against 22.5 for Northway and 21.2 for ParcelPro.
- Parcels shipped on Mondays take longest, because of the weekend backlog.
- Overall, 17% of deliveries arrived after the time promised to the customer.
- ParcelPro only started in September, so its figures rest on 40 deliveries, against 90 for each of the others. Its single delivery over 48 hours could easily be two or three in a larger sample.
- Delivery time rises with distance (correlation 0.39 for deliveries under 48 hours).

```python
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = pd.read_csv('data.csv')
df['over48'] = df['actual_hours'] > 48

summary = (
    df.groupby('courier')
      .agg(n=('delivery_id', 'size'),
           over48=('over48', 'sum'),
           median_hours=('actual_hours', 'median'))
      .reset_index()
)
summary['pct'] = 100 * summary['over48'] / summary['n']
summary = summary.sort_values('pct', ascending=True)  # highest bar at top for barh

color_map = {'Northway': '#4C72B0', 'ParcelPro': '#55A868', 'Swiftline': '#C44E52'}
colors = [color_map[c] for c in summary['courier']]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
bars = ax.barh(summary['courier'], summary['pct'], color=colors, height=0.55)

ax.set_xlabel('Deliveries exceeding 48 hours (%)', fontsize=12)
ax.set_xlim(0, max(summary['pct']) * 1.35)
ax.spines['top'].set_visible(False)
ax.spines['right'].set_visible(False)
ax.grid(axis='x', alpha=0.25)
ax.set_axisbelow(True)
ax.tick_params(axis='y', labelsize=12)
ax.tick_params(axis='x', labelsize=11)

for bar, (_, row) in zip(bars, summary.iterrows()):
    x = bar.get_width()
    ax.text(
        x + max(summary['pct']) * 0.02,
        bar.get_y() + bar.get_height() / 2,
        f"{row['pct']:.1f}%  ({int(row['over48'])}/{int(row['n'])})",
        va='center', ha='left', fontsize=11, fontweight='bold'
    )

ax.set_title(
    'Refrigerated medicine: risk of a cold-chain breach',
    fontsize=15, fontweight='bold', pad=18
)
ax.text(
    0.0, 1.02,
    'Share of deliveries taking longer than the 48-hour cold-pack limit',
    transform=ax.transAxes, fontsize=11, color='#444444',
    ha='left', va='bottom'
)

swift_med = summary.loc[summary['courier'] == 'Swiftline', 'median_hours'].iloc[0]
ax.text(
    0.62, 0.28,
    f"Swiftline is typically fastest\n(median {swift_med:.1f}h), but has\n~7× the >48h risk.",
    transform=ax.transAxes, fontsize=10.5, ha='left', va='center',
    bbox=dict(boxstyle='round,pad=0.5', fc='#FFF8E1', ec='#D9A400', alpha=0.95)
)

fig.text(
    0.5, 0.02,
    'Prices and customer ratings are similar; each courier damaged one parcel. '
    'ParcelPro has only 40 deliveries, so its estimate is less certain.',
    ha='center', fontsize=9, color='#555555'
)

plt.tight_layout(rect=[0, 0.05, 1, 0.93])
```

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = pd.read_csv("data.csv")
df["format"] = df["format"].str.strip()

format_colors = {"standard": "#2E86AB", "large": "#F18F01"}

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 6))

# Left panel: sales per sq ft vs floor area
for fmt, color in format_colors.items():
    subset = df[df["format"] == fmt]

        subset["sq_ft"],
        subset["sales_per_sqft_usd"],
        s=subset["annual_sales_musd"] * 8,
        alpha=0.7,
        color=color,
        edgecolor="white",
        linewidth=0.7,
        label=f"{fmt.title()} stores"
    )

for fmt, color in format_colors.items():
    mean_sp = df.loc[df["format"] == fmt, "sales_per_sqft_usd"].mean()
    ax1.axhline(mean_sp, color=color, linestyle="--", linewidth=1, alpha=0.6)

s39 = df[df["store_id"] == "S39"].iloc[0]
ax1.annotate(
    f"S39: top seller\n${s39['annual_sales_musd']:.1f}m sales",
    xy=(s39["sq_ft"], s39["sales_per_sqft_usd"]),
    xytext=(10, 10),

    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", lw=0.8)
)

for _, row in new_large.iterrows():

large_all_mean = df.loc[df["format"] == "large", "sales_per_sqft_usd"].mean()
```

## Analyst notes
- Courier prices are within 50 cents of each other ($9.28 to $9.73 per delivery).
- Customer ratings are similar (4.2 to 4.3 out of 5).
- Cold packs keep these medicines safe for 48 hours. Swiftline delivered 14.4% of parcels after more than 48 hours, against 2.2% for Northway and 2.5% for ParcelPro.
- Each courier damaged one parcel.
- Rural deliveries take about 4 hours longer than urban and suburban ones.
- Swiftline is fastest on a typical delivery: a median of 17.9 hours, against 22.5 for Northway and 21.2 for ParcelPro.
- Parcels shipped on Mondays take longest, because of the weekend backlog.
- Overall, 17% of deliveries arrived after the time promised to the customer.
- ParcelPro only started in September, so its figures rest on 40 deliveries, against 90 for each of the others. Its single delivery over 48 hours could easily be two or three in a larger sample.
- Delivery time rises with distance (correlation 0.39 for deliveries under 48 hours).

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = pd.read_csv("data.csv")
df["over48"] = df["actual_hours"] > 48

order = ["ParcelPro", "Northway", "Swiftline"]  # bottom to top

g = df.groupby("courier").agg(
    n=("delivery_id", "size"),
    n_over=("over48", "sum"),
    median_h=("actual_hours", "median"),
    cost=("cost_usd", "mean"),
    rating=("customer_rating", "mean"),
    damaged=("damaged", "sum"),
).loc[order]
g["pct_over"] = 100 * g["n_over"] / g["n"]

colors = {"Swiftline": "#C1272D", "Northway": "#1B6B6B", "ParcelPro": "#7A8A99"}
bar_colors = [colors[c] for c in g.index]

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(
    1, 2, figsize=(10, 6),

)

# --- Title: the decision, readable in 10 seconds ---

    fontsize=19, fontweight="bold", x=0.5, y=0.97, ha="center",
)
fig.text(

    "Cold packs last 48 hours.  One in seven Swiftline parcels arrived after that.",
    fontsize=12.5, ha="center", color="#333333",

y = np.arange(len(g))

    label = f"{pct:.1f}%   ({int(n_over)} of {int(n)})"
    if courier == "Swiftline":
        label += "  —  1 in 7 unsafe"
    ax1.text(
        pct + 0.4, yi, label,
        va="center", ha="left", fontsize=12.5,
        fontweight="bold" if courier == "Swiftline" else "normal",
        color=colors[courier] if courier == "Swiftline" else "#222222",
    )

ax1.set_yticks(y)
ax1.set_yticklabels(
    [f"{c}\n(n={int(g.loc[c, 'n'])})" for c in g.index], fontsize=11.5
)
ax1.set_xlim(0, 19)
ax1.set_xticks([0, 5, 10, 15])
ax1.set_xticklabels(["0%", "5%", "10%", "15%"], fontsize=10)
ax1.set_xlabel("Parcels delivered after 48 hours", fontsize=11)
ax1.set_title("UNSAFE DELIVERIES  (> 48 h)", fontsize=12, fontweight="bold", pad=10)
ax1.spines[["top", "right", "left"]].set_visible(False)
ax1.tick_params(length=0)
ax1.grid(axis="x", color="#DDDDDD", linewidth=0.7)
ax1.set_axisbelow(True)

ax2.barh(y, g["median_h"], height=0.55, color=bar_colors, edgecolor="none", alpha=0.9)
ax2.axvline(48, color="#C1272D", linestyle="--", linewidth=1.6)
ax2.text(48.6, len(g) - 0.35, "48 h\ncold-pack\nlimit",
         fontsize=9, color="#C1272D", va="top", ha="left")

for yi, courier in zip(y, g.index):
    med = g.loc[courier, "median_h"]
    ax2.text(med + 1, yi, f"{med:.1f} h", va="center", ha="left", fontsize=12)

ax2.set_yticklabels([])
ax2.set_xlim(0, 60)

cost_lo, cost_hi = g["cost"].min(), g["cost"].max()
```

- Rural deliveries take about 4 hours longer than urban and suburban ones.

- Parcels shipped on Mondays take longest, because of the weekend backlog.
- Overall, 17% of deliveries arrived after the time promised to the customer.
- ParcelPro only started in September, so its figures rest on 40 deliveries, against 90 for each of the others. Its single delivery over 48 hours could easily be two or three in a larger sample.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D

df = pd.read_csv("data.csv")

order = ["Swiftline", "Northway", "ParcelPro"]
df = df[df["courier"].isin(order)].copy()

# Summary statistics, calculated from the data
summary = (
    df.groupby("courier")
    .agg(
        n=("actual_hours", "size"),
        median=("actual_hours", "median"),
        over48=("actual_hours", lambda x: (x > 48).sum()),
        mean_cost=("cost_usd", "mean"),
        mean_rating=("customer_rating", "mean"),
        damaged=("damaged", "sum"),
    )
    .reindex(order)
)
summary["pct_over48"] = 100 * summary["over48"] / summary["n"]

# Wilson 95% confidence intervals for % over 48 hours
z = 1.96
ci_low, ci_high = [], []
for _, row in summary.iterrows():
    n, k = row["n"], row["over48"]
    p = k / n
    denom = 1 + z**2 / n
    centre = (p + z**2 / (2 * n)) / denom
    half = z * np.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n + z**2 / (4 * n**2)) / denom
    ci_low.append(100 * max(0, centre - half))
    ci_high.append(100 * min(1, centre + half))
summary["ci_low"] = ci_low
summary["ci_high"] = ci_high

fig, (ax, ax2) = plt.subplots(
    1, 2,
    figsize=(10, 6),
    sharey=True,
    gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [2.35, 1.0], "wspace": 0.08},
)

fig.suptitle(
    "Swiftline is fastest on a typical delivery — but most often outlasts the cold pack",
    fontsize=14, fontweight="bold", x=0.06, ha="left",
)
fig.text(
    0.06, 0.92,
    "Medicines stay safe for 48 hours. Swiftline's low median hides a long, unsafe tail.",
    fontsize=10.5, color="#444444", ha="left",
)

# --- Left panel: every delivery ---
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
colours = {"safe": "#4C78A8", "unsafe": "#C1272D"}

y_labels = []
for i, courier in enumerate(order):
    sub = df[df["courier"] == courier]
    y = i + rng.uniform(-0.18, 0.18, size=len(sub))
    safe = sub["actual_hours"] <= 48

    ax.scatter(
        sub.loc[safe, "actual_hours"], y[safe.values],
        s=22, color=colours["safe"], alpha=0.55,
        edgecolors="white", linewidths=0.4, zorder=3,
    )
    ax.scatter(
        sub.loc[~safe, "actual_hours"], y[(~safe).values],
        s=34, color=colours["unsafe"], alpha=0.9,
        edgecolors="white", linewidths=0.5, zorder=4,
    )

    med = summary.loc[courier, "median"]
    ax.plot([med, med], [i - 0.30, i + 0.30], color="black", lw=3, zorder=5)
    y_labels.append(
        f"{courier}\nmedian {med:.1f} h, n={int(summary.loc[courier, 'n'])}"
    )

ax.axvline(48, color=colours["unsafe"], lw=1.8, ls="--", zorder=2)
ax.text(
    48.7, -0.62, "48-hour\ncold-pack limit",
    color=colours["unsafe"], fontsize=8.5, va="bottom", fontweight="bold",
)
ax.set_xlim(0, 82)
ax.set_xlabel("Actual time from dispatch to delivery (hours)")
ax.set_title("Every delivery", fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", loc="left")
ax.set_yticks(range(len(order)))
ax.set_yticklabels(y_labels)
ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.set_ylim(len(order) - 0.35, -0.65)
ax.grid(axis="x", color="#DDDDDD", lw=0.6)
ax.set_axisbelow(True)

legend_handles = [
    Line2D([0], [0], marker="o", color="w", markerfacecolor=colours["safe"],
           markersize=6, label="Delivered within 48 h"),
    Line2D([0], [0], marker="o", color="w", markerfacecolor=colours["unsafe"],
           markersize=7, label="Delivered after 48 h"),
    Line2D([0], [0], color="black", lw=3, label="Median"),
]
ax.legend(handles=legend_handles, frameon=False, fontsize=8.5, loc="lower right")

# --- Right panel: share beyond the safety limit ---
bar_colours = ["#C1272D", "#7A7A7A", "#7A7A7A"]
y_pos = np.arange(len(order))
pcts = summary["pct_over48"].values
xerr = np.vstack([
    pcts - summary["ci_low"].values,
    summary["ci_high"].values - pcts,
])
ax2.barh(y_pos, pcts, color=bar_colours, height=0.52, zorder=3)
ax2.errorbar(
    pcts, y_pos, xerr=xerr, fmt="none",
    ecolor="black", elinewidth=1.1, capsize=3, zorder=4,
)
for i, courier in enumerate(order):
    row = summary.loc[courier]
    ax2.text(
        row["ci_high"] + 0.7, i,
        f"{row['pct_over48']:.1f}%  ({int(row['over48'])}/{int(row['n'])})",
        va="center", fontsize=9,
        fontweight="bold" if courier == "Swiftline" else "normal",
    )

ax2.set_xlim(0, 27)
ax2.set_xlabel("Deliveries taking >48 hours (%)")
ax2.set_title("Beyond the safety limit", fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", loc="left")
ax2.grid(axis="x", color="#DDDDDD", lw=0.6)
ax2.set_axisbelow(True)

for a in (ax, ax2):
    for spine in ("top", "right"):
        a.spines[spine].set_visible(False)

cost_lo, cost_hi = summary["mean_cost"].min(), summary["mean_cost"].max()
rate_lo, rate_hi = summary["mean_rating"].min(), summary["mean_rating"].max()
fig.text(
    0.06, 0.02,
    "Each dot is one delivery (n=220, Aug–Oct 2026). Error bars are 95% Wilson intervals; ParcelPro "
    "only started in September (n=40), so its estimate is less certain.\n"
    f"Couriers were otherwise similar: mean cost ${cost_lo:.2f}–${cost_hi:.2f}, "
    f"mean rating {rate_lo:.1f}–{rate_hi:.1f}/5, and one damaged parcel each.",
    fontsize=8.5, color="#555555", ha="left", va="bottom",
)

fig.tight_layout(rect=[0, 0.07, 1, 0.89])
```

## Analyst notes
- Courier prices are within 50 cents of each other ($9.28 to $9.73 per delivery).
- Customer ratings are similar (4.2 to 4.3 out of 5).
- Cold packs keep these medicines safe for 48 hours. Swiftline delivered 14.4% of parcels after more than 48 hours, against 2.2% for Northway and 2.5% for ParcelPro.
- Each courier damaged one parcel.
- Rural deliveries take about 4 hours longer than urban and suburban ones.
- Swiftline is fastest on a typical delivery: a median of 17.9 hours, against 22.5 for Northway and 21.2 for ParcelPro.
- Parcels shipped on Mondays take longest, because of the weekend backlog.
- Overall, 17% of deliveries arrived after the time promised to the customer.
- ParcelPro only started in September, so its figures rest on 40 deliveries, against 90 for each of the others. Its single delivery over 48 hours could easily be two or three in a larger sample.
- Delivery time rises with distance (correlation 0.39 for deliveries under 48 hours).

- Each courier damaged one parcel.
- Rural deliveries take about 4 hours longer than urban and suburban ones.
- Swiftline is fastest on a typical delivery: a median of 17.9 hours, against 22.5 for Northway and 21.2 for ParcelPro.
- Parcels shipped on Mondays take longest, because of the weekend backlog.
- Overall, 17% of deliveries arrived after the time promised to the customer.
- ParcelPro only started in September, so its figures rest on 40 deliveries, against 90 for each of the others. Its single delivery over 48 hours could easily be two or three in a larger sample.
- Delivery time rises with distance (correlation 0.39 for deliveries under 48 hours).

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("data.csv")

# For refrigerated medicine, only the tail beyond the 48-hour
# cold-pack limit matters for safety — not typical speed.
summary = (
    df.groupby("courier")
    .agg(pct_over_48=("actual_hours", lambda s: (s > 48).mean() * 100),
         n=("actual_hours", "size"),
         n_over=("actual_hours", lambda s: (s > 48).sum()))
    .reindex(["Swiftline", "ParcelPro", "Northway"])
)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))

couriers = summary.index.tolist()
values = summary["pct_over_48"].values
labels = [f"{c}  (n={int(summary.loc[c, 'n'])})" for c in couriers]
colors = ["#C1272D" if c == "Swiftline" else "#B8B8B8" for c in couriers]

ax.barh(labels, values, color=colors, height=0.55)
ax.invert_yaxis()

ax.set_xlim(0, max(values) * 1.35)
ax.set_xlabel("Deliveries taking more than 48 hours (%)", fontsize=11)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=12, length=0)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=11)
ax.xaxis.grid(True, color="#E6E6E6", linewidth=0.8)
ax.set_axisbelow(True)
for spine in ["top", "right", "left"]:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)

# Only the number that carries the message is labelled
swift = summary.loc["Swiftline"]
ax.text(swift["pct_over_48"] + 0.4, 0,
        f"{swift['pct_over_48']:.1f}%  ({int(swift['n_over'])} of {int(swift['n'])})",
        va="center", ha="left", fontsize=13, fontweight="bold", color="#C1272D")

ax.set_title("Swiftline puts 1 in 7 refrigerated deliveries past the 48-hour safety limit",
             loc="left", fontsize=16, fontweight="bold", pad=14)

pp = summary.loc["ParcelPro"]
fig.text(0.07, 0.03,
         f"Cold packs keep medicines safe for 48 hours. ParcelPro started in September "
         f"({int(pp['n'])} deliveries vs 90 each for the others),\n"
         f"so its figure rests on {int(pp['n_over'])} late parcel and is less certain. "
         f"Cost and customer ratings are similar across couriers.",
         fontsize=9, color="#555555", ha="left", va="bottom")

plt.tight_layout(rect=[0, 0.09, 1, 0.96])
```

Design guidance:
- Pick the one message the audience most needs for this decision, and make the title state it as a sentence.
- Show only the data needed for that message. Leave out series, columns and notes that do not help the decision.
- Use one strong colour for what matters and grey for context. Label lines or bars directly instead of using a legend when you can.
- Add a number label only where the number is part of the message. Do not label every bar or point.
- If a caveat changes how the chart should be read, state it briefly on the chart.
- Keep scales honest: bar charts start at zero, units are labelled, no 3-D effects and no second y-axis.

## Output

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.ticker import FuncFormatter

# Load data
df = pd.read_csv('data.csv')

# Group definitions for the comparison
standard = df[df['format'] == 'standard']
large_established = df[(df['format'] == 'large') & (df['opened_year'] < 2025)]
large_new = df[(df['format'] == 'large') & (df['opened_year'] >= 2025)]

groups = [
    (f"Standard\n(n={len(standard)})", standard['sales_per_sqft_usd'].mean(), '#0B6E4F'),
    (f"Large, opened\nbefore 2025\n(n={len(large_established)})", large_established['sales_per_sqft_usd'].mean(), '#BDBDBD'),
    (f"Large, opened\n2025–26\n(n={len(large_new)})", large_new['sales_per_sqft_usd'].mean(), '#BDBDBD'),
]

labels = [g[0] for g in groups]
values = [g[1] for g in groups]
colors = [g[2] for g in groups]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
bars = ax.bar(labels, values, color=colors, width=0.6)

# Direct value labels
for bar, val in zip(bars, values):
    ax.text(
        bar.get_x() + bar.get_width() / 2,
        val + 10,
        f"${val:,.0f}",
        ha='center',
        va='bottom',
        fontsize=14,
        fontweight='bold',
        color='#222222'
    )

# Title states the key message
ax.set_title(
    "Standard stores sell more per square foot than established large stores;\nnew large stores lag further",
    fontsize=15,
    fontweight='bold',
    loc='left',
    pad=16
)

ax.set_ylabel("Annual sales per square foot (USD)", fontsize=11)
ax.set_ylim(0, 700)
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(FuncFormatter(lambda x, p: f"${x:,.0f}"))
ax.tick_params(axis='x', labelsize=11, pad=6)
ax.tick_params(axis='y', labelsize=10)

# Clean, honest scales
ax.grid(axis='y', color='#DDDDDD', linewidth=0.8)
ax.set_axisbelow(True)
for spine in ['top', 'right']:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
ax.spines['left'].set_color('#888888')
ax.spines['bottom'].set_color('#888888')

# Brief caveat
fig.text(
    0.01, 0.01,
    "Note: Large stores opened in 2025–26 are still ramping up; compare standard with established large stores.",
    fontsize=9,
    color='#555555',
    ha='left',
    va='bottom'
)

plt.tight_layout(rect=[0, 0.05, 1, 0.95])
```

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = pd.read_csv("data.csv")

quarters = sorted(df["quarter"].unique())
qpos = {q: i for i, q in enumerate(quarters)}

GREY = "#b8b8b8"

)

for cat, g in df.groupby("category"):

        continue
    ax1.plot(g["x"], g["return_rate_pct"], color=GREY, lw=1.3, zorder=1)

fw = df[df["category"] == "Footwear"].sort_values("x")
ax1.plot(fw["x"], fw["return_rate_pct"], color=HILITE, lw=2.6,
         marker="o", ms=4, zorder=3)
last = fw.iloc[-1]
ax1.annotate(f"Footwear\n{last['return_rate_pct']:.1f}%",
             xy=(last["x"], last["return_rate_pct"]),
             xytext=(-12, 8), textcoords="offset points",
             ha="right", va="bottom", color=HILITE, fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")

for cat in ["Swimwear", "Accessories"]:
    g = df[df["category"] == cat].sort_values("x")
    ax1.text(g["x"].iloc[0], g["return_rate_pct"].iloc[0] + 0.6, cat,
             color="#808080", fontsize=8.5, ha="left", va="bottom")
ax1.text(0, 14.6, "Other categories (grey)", color="#808080", fontsize=8.5)

ax1.set_xticks(range(len(quarters)))
ax1.set_xticklabels(qlabels, fontsize=9)

ax1.set_ylim(0, 27)
ax1.set_title("Return rate by category", loc="left", fontsize=11)
ax1.grid(axis="y", color="#eeeeee")
ax1.set_axisbelow(True)

# Right panel: Footwear return rate split into defect vs other returns
defect_pts = fw["return_rate_pct"] * fw["defect_share_of_returns_pct"] / 100
other_pts = fw["return_rate_pct"] - defect_pts
x = np.arange(len(fw))
ax2.bar(x, other_pts, color=GREY, width=0.65, label="Other reasons (mostly size/fit)")
ax2.bar(x, defect_pts, bottom=other_pts, color=HILITE, width=0.65,
        label="Customer reported a defect")

for xi, tot, d in zip(x, fw["return_rate_pct"], defect_pts):
    ax2.text(xi, tot + 0.3, f"{tot:.1f}%", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=8.5)

ax2.annotate("46% of Q3 2026 returns\nreported a defect,\nmostly soles coming apart",
             xy=(x[-1] - 0.33, other_pts.iloc[-1] + defect_pts.iloc[-1] / 2),
             xytext=(x[-1] - 1.5, 15.5), ha="right", va="center",
             fontsize=8.5, color=HILITE,
             arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=HILITE, lw=0.8))

ax2.set_xticks(x)
ax2.set_xticklabels([qlabels[i] for i in fw["x"]], fontsize=9)
ax2.set_ylim(0, 27)
ax2.set_ylabel("Footwear return rate (percentage points)")

ax2.legend(loc="upper left", frameon=False, fontsize=8.5)
ax2.grid(axis="y", color="#eeeeee")
ax2.set_axisbelow(True)
```

```python
df = pd.read_csv("data.csv")

# Defect-related returns as a share of units sold: the direct measure of a quality problem
df["defect_returns"] = df["units_returned"] * df["defect_share_of_returns_pct"] / 100
df["defect_return_rate"] = df["defect_returns"] / df["units_sold"] * 100

quarters = sorted(df["quarter"].unique())
xpos = {q: i for i, q in enumerate(quarters)}
```

## Analyst notes
- Courier prices are within 50 cents of each other ($9.28 to $9.73 per delivery).
- Customer ratings are similar (4.2 to 4.3 out of 5).
- Cold packs keep these medicines safe for 48 hours. Swiftline delivered 14.4% of parcels after more than 48 hours, against 2.2% for Northway and 2.5% for ParcelPro.
- Each courier damaged one parcel.
- Rural deliveries take about 4 hours longer than urban and suburban ones.
- Swiftline is fastest on a typical delivery: a median of 17.9 hours, against 22.5 for Northway and 21.2 for ParcelPro.
- Parcels shipped on Mondays take longest, because of the weekend backlog.
- Overall, 17% of deliveries arrived after the time promised to the customer.
- ParcelPro only started in September, so its figures rest on 40 deliveries, against 90 for each of the others. Its single delivery over 48 hours could easily be two or three in a larger sample.
- Delivery time rises with distance (correlation 0.39 for deliveries under 48 hours).

- Accessories have the lowest return rate, around 3%.
- Footwear's return rate jumped to 19.2% in Q3 2026, from an average of 10.8% over the previous six quarters. No other category moved by more than 0.9 points.

```python
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Read the data
df = pd.read_csv('data.csv')

# Previous six quarters (all except Q3 2026)
prev_quarters = ['2025Q1', '2025Q2', '2025Q3', '2025Q4', '2026Q1', '2026Q2']

# Average return rate over previous quarters for each category
prev_avg = df[df['quarter'].isin(prev_quarters)].groupby('category')['return_rate_pct'].mean()

# Q3 2026 return rate for each category
q3_2026 = df[df['quarter'] == '2026Q3'].set_index('category')['return_rate_pct']

# Change from prior average
change = (q3_2026 - prev_avg).dropna()
change_sorted = change.sort_values(ascending=False)

# Colors: strong red for Footwear, grey for context
colors = ['#D62728' if cat == 'Footwear' else '#B0B0B0' for cat in change_sorted.index]

# Create figure
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))

# Horizontal bars
ax.barh(change_sorted.index, change_sorted.values, color=colors, edgecolor='none')

# Put the largest (Footwear) at the top
ax.invert_yaxis()

# Zero reference line
ax.axvline(0, color='black', linewidth=0.8, alpha=0.5)

# Set x-axis limits to fit annotation
min_change = change_sorted.min()
max_change = change_sorted.max()
ax.set_xlim(min_change - 1.5, max_change + 7)

# Footwear annotation
footwear_change = change_sorted['Footwear']
footwear_q3_rate = q3_2026['Footwear']
footwear_q3_defect = df[(df['category'] == 'Footwear') & (df['quarter'] == '2026Q3')]['defect_share_of_returns_pct'].values[0]

text_x = footwear_change + 0.3
text_y = 0  # Footwear is at y=0 after invert

        va='center', ha='left', fontsize=10, color='#D62728', fontweight='bold')

# Axis labels and ticks
ax.set_xlabel('Change in return rate (percentage points)', fontsize=10)
ax.set_ylabel('')
ax.tick_params(axis='y', labelsize=10)
ax.tick_params(axis='x', labelsize=9)

# Title and subtitle
title = "Investigate Footwear first: its Q3 2026 return rate jumped to 19.2%, driven by defects"
subtitle = "Change in return rate vs prior 6-quarter average."
fig.text(0.01, 0.97, title, fontsize=14, fontweight='bold', ha='left', va='top')
fig.text(0.01, 0.92, subtitle, fontsize=10, color='gray', ha='left', va='top')

# Caveat

ax.spines['top'].set_visible(False)
ax.spines['right'].set_visible(False)

# Layout adjustments
plt.subplots_adjust(top=0.85, bottom=0.15, left=0.18, right=0.95)
```

```python
ax.step(dates, opt, where="mid", color=C_OPT, lw=2, ls="--", zorder=2)

short = act > cap
```

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle

df = pd.read_csv("data.csv")

# Point change in % favourable, 2025 -> 2026, for each department x question
wide = df.pivot_table(index=["department", "question"], columns="year",
                      values="pct_favourable")
change = (wide[2026] - wide[2025]).unstack("question")

questions = [
    "My manager supports my growth",
    "I see myself working here in two years",
    "I would recommend Northlight as a place to work",
    "I have the tools I need to do my job",
    "My workload is manageable",
    "I understand the company's strategy",
]
q_labels = [
    "Manager supports\nmy growth",
    "See myself here\nin two years",
    "Would recommend\nNorthlight",
    "Have the tools\nI need",
    "Workload is\nmanageable",
    "Understand company\nstrategy",
]

# Customer Support first, then the rest by headcount (largest first)
info = df.groupby(["department", "year"])[["response_rate_pct", "n_responses", "headcount"]].first()
heads = df.groupby("department")["headcount"].first().sort_values(ascending=False)
depts = ["Customer Support"] + [d for d in heads.index if d != "Customer Support"]

mat = change.loc[depts, questions].values

row_labels = []
for d in depts:
    r26 = info.loc[(d, 2026), "response_rate_pct"]
    r25 = info.loc[(d, 2025), "response_rate_pct"]
    if d == "Customer Support":
        row_labels.append(f"{d}\n{r26}% responded (was {r25}%)")
    else:
        row_labels.append(f"{d}  ({r26}% responded)")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))

        weight = "bold" if abs(v) >= 15 else "normal"
        ax.text(j, i, txt, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=10,
                color=color, fontweight=weight)

ax.set_xticks(range(len(questions)))
ax.set_xticklabels(q_labels, fontsize=9)
ax.xaxis.tick_top()
ax.set_yticks(range(len(depts)))
ax.set_yticklabels(row_labels, fontsize=9)
```

## Analyst notes
- Across all 90 days the forecast was off by 1.3% on average.
- Wind speed has almost no relation to peak demand (correlation -0.02).
- The forecast under-predicts demand on very cold days. On the 7 days below −15 °C, actual peak demand was 5.3% above the forecast on average (about 47 MW).
- Weekend peaks are about 12% lower than weekday peaks.
- The share of demand from homes rises in cold weather.
- Peak demand exceeded available capacity on 4 days, 12 to 15 January, and the shortfall was covered with emergency imports.
- Imports at the daily peak averaged 22 MW.
- Unit 3 (50 MW) was out for repair from 10 to 16 January, cutting available capacity from 960 to 910 MW. With Unit 3 running, only 14 January would have exceeded capacity.
- The highest peak of the winter was 1,012 MW on 14 January.
- On mild days (above −3 °C) the forecast slightly over-predicts, by 1.8% on average.

```python
df = pd.read_csv("data.csv")
```

```python
RED = "#C0392B"

DARK = "#333333"

questions = [
    "My manager supports my growth",
    "I see myself working here in two years",
]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 6), sharey=True)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.08, right=0.97, top=0.78, bottom=0.17, wspace=0.12)

for i, (ax, q) in enumerate(zip(axes, questions)):
    piv = (df[df["question"] == q]
           .pivot(index="department", columns="year", values="pct_favourable"))

    # Other departments in grey, for context
    for dept, row in piv.iterrows():
        if dept == FOCUS:
            continue
        ax.plot([0, 1], [row[2025], row[2026]], color=GREY, lw=1.3,
                marker="o", ms=4, zorder=1)

    # Customer Support highlighted
    v25, v26 = piv.loc[FOCUS, 2025], piv.loc[FOCUS, 2026]
    change = v26 - v25
    ax.plot([0, 1], [v25, v26], color=RED, lw=3.2, marker="o", ms=7, zorder=3)
    ax.text(-0.06, v25, f"{v25:.0f}%", color=RED, fontsize=12,
```
