```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = pd.read_csv("data.csv")
df["month_dt"] = pd.to_datetime(df["month"] + "-01")

channels = ["Branch", "Online", "Broker", "Partner app"]
colors = {"Branch": "#4C72B0", "Online": "#55A868", "Broker": "#C44E52", "Partner app": "#8172B2"}

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 6), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.25, 1]})

# Left panel: monthly funded value by channel
pv = df.pivot(index="month_dt", columns="channel", values="funded_value_musd")
for ch in channels:
    s = pv[ch].dropna()
    ax1.plot(s.index, s.values, marker="o", ms=4, lw=2, color=colors[ch])
    ax1.annotate(f"{ch}\n${s.iloc[-1]:.1f}M", xy=(s.index[-1], s.values[-1]),
                 xytext=(6, 0), textcoords="offset points", va="center",
                 fontsize=9, color=colors[ch], fontweight="bold")

partner_start = pv["Partner app"].first_valid_index()
ax1.annotate("Partner app\nlaunched", xy=(partner_start, pv.loc[partner_start, "Partner app"]),
             xytext=(0, 22), textcoords="offset points", ha="center", fontsize=8,
             color=colors["Partner app"], arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=colors["Partner app"], lw=0.8))

ax1.set_ylim(0, 16)
ax1.set_ylabel("Funded value, $ millions")
ax1.set_title("Funded value per month", loc="left", fontsize=11)
months = pv.index
ax1.set_xticks(months)
ax1.set_xticklabels([m.strftime("%b") for m in months])
ax1.set_xlim(months[0] - pd.Timedelta(days=10), months[-1] + pd.Timedelta(days=75))
ax1.grid(axis="y", alpha=0.3)
for sp in ["top", "right"]:
    ax1.spines[sp].set_visible(False)

# Right panel: acquisition cost per $100 lent (Jan–Sep totals)
df["total_cost"] = df["acquisition_cost_per_loan_usd"] * df["funded_loans"]
agg = df.groupby("channel").agg(total_cost=("total_cost", "sum"),
                                value=("funded_value_musd", "sum"),
                                loans=("funded_loans", "sum"))
agg["cost_per_100"] = agg["total_cost"] / (agg["value"] * 1e6) * 100
agg["cost_per_loan"] = agg["total_cost"] / agg["loans"]
agg["avg_loan_k"] = agg["value"] * 1e3 / agg["loans"]
agg = agg.loc[channels].sort_values("cost_per_100")

y = np.arange(len(agg))
ax2.barh(y, agg["cost_per_100"], color=[colors[c] for c in agg.index], height=0.6)
for i, (ch, r) in enumerate(agg.iterrows()):
    ax2.text(r["cost_per_100"] + 0.06, i, f"${r['cost_per_100']:.2f}",
             va="center", fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")
    ax2.text(0.08, i - 0.42,
             f"${r['cost_per_loan']:,.0f} per loan · avg loan ${r['avg_loan_k']:.0f}k",
             va="center", fontsize=8, color="#444444")
ax2.set_yticks(y)
ax2.set_yticklabels(agg.index)
ax2.set_xlim(0, agg["cost_per_100"].max() * 1.25)
ax2.set_ylim(-0.75, len(agg) - 0.5)
ax2.set_xlabel("Acquisition cost per $100 lent, US dollars")
ax2.set_title("Acquisition cost per $100 lent, Jan–Sep", loc="left", fontsize=11)
ax2.grid(axis="x", alpha=0.3)
for sp in ["top", "right"]:
    ax2.spines[sp].set_visible(False)

fig.suptitle("Broker costs most per loan, but per dollar lent branches are the costliest channel",
             fontsize=13, fontweight="bold", x=0.02, ha="left")
fig.text(0.02, 0.01,
         "Acquisition cost = marketing, commission and processing. Partner app launched March 2026. "
         "Total funded value Jan–Sep 2026: ${:.0f}M.".format(df["funded_value_musd"].sum()),
         fontsize=8, color="#555555")
fig.tight_layout(rect=[0, 0.03, 1, 0.94])
```

```python
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = pd.read_csv("data.csv")

# Aggregate Jan to Sep 2026 by channel
df["acq_cost_total"] = df["funded_loans"] * df["acquisition_cost_per_loan_usd"]
g = df.groupby("channel").agg(
    loans=("funded_loans", "sum"),
    value_musd=("funded_value_musd", "sum"),
    cost=("acq_cost_total", "sum"),
)
g["cost_per_loan"] = g["cost"] / g["loans"]
g["cost_per_100"] = g["cost"] / (g["value_musd"] * 1e6) * 100

order = ["Branch", "Online", "Partner app", "Broker"]   # Broker at the top of the horizontal bars
g = g.loc[order]

broker_share = g.loc["Broker", "value_musd"] / g["value_musd"].sum() * 100
total_value = g["value_musd"].sum()

HIGHLIGHT = "#C0392B"
GREY = "#B8B8B8"
colors = [HIGHLIGHT if c == "Broker" else GREY for c in order]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 6), sharey=True)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.12, right=0.96, top=0.74, bottom=0.17, wspace=0.12)

panels = [
    ("cost_per_loan", "Cost per funded loan (US$)", lambda v: f"${v:,.0f}"),
    ("cost_per_100", "Cost per $100 lent (US$)", lambda v: f"${v:.2f}"),
]

for ax, (col, label, fmt) in zip(axes, panels):
    vals = g[col].values
    ax.barh(order, vals, color=colors, height=0.6)
    ax.set_xlim(0, vals.max() * 1.25)
    ax.set_title(label, loc="left", fontsize=12, fontweight="bold", color="#333333")
    for i, (c, v) in enumerate(zip(order, vals)):
        is_b = c == "Broker"

                fontsize=12 if is_b else 10,

    ax.xaxis.set_visible(False)
    for s in ["top", "right", "bottom"]:
        ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
    ax.spines["left"].set_color("#999999")
    ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=0, labelsize=11)

for lbl in axes[0].get_yticklabels():

fig.text(0.02, 0.95,
```

```python
import numpy as np
```

```python
monthly_filled = monthly.fillna(0)  # only for stacking totals; Partner app did not exist Jan-Feb

totals = monthly_filled.sum(axis=1)

).reindex(channels)
```

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = pd.read_csv("data.csv")
df["date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["month"])
df["days"] = df["date"].dt.days_in_month

# Restriction period: June-September
rest = df[df["date"] >= "2026-06-01"].copy()
rest["excess_ml"] = (
    (rest["litres_per_household_day"] - rest["target_lphd"])
    * rest["households"] * rest["days"] / 1e6
)

rows = []
for district, g in rest.groupby("district"):

        "avg": avg,
        "target": target,
        "pct_over": (avg / target - 1) * 100,
        "excess_ml": g["excess_ml"].sum(),

s = pd.DataFrame(rows).sort_values("pct_over", ascending=True).reset_index(drop=True)
```

## Analyst notes
- Courier prices are within 50 cents of each other ($9.28 to $9.73 per delivery).
- Customer ratings are similar (4.2 to 4.3 out of 5).
- Cold packs keep these medicines safe for 48 hours. Swiftline delivered 14.4% of parcels after more than 48 hours, against 2.2% for Northway and 2.5% for ParcelPro.
- Each courier damaged one parcel.
- Rural deliveries take about 4 hours longer than urban and suburban ones.
- Swiftline is fastest on a typical delivery: a median of 17.9 hours, against 22.5 for Northway and 21.2 for ParcelPro.
- Parcels shipped on Mondays take longest, because of the weekend backlog.
- Overall, 17% of deliveries arrived after the time promised to the customer.
- ParcelPro only started in September, so its figures rest on 40 deliveries, against 90 for each of the others. Its single delivery over 48 hours could easily be two or three in a larger sample.
- Delivery time rises with distance (correlation 0.39 for deliveries under 48 hours).

- A bug that hid the payment button on some phones in the new checkout was fixed on 26 September. Mobile conversion on the new checkout was 2.24% on 26 and 27 September, close to the old checkout, but two days is too short to judge.

- Both versions dipped on 20 September during a payment-provider outage.

## Analyst notes
- Courier prices are within 50 cents of each other ($9.28 to $9.73 per delivery).
- Customer ratings are similar (4.2 to 4.3 out of 5).
- Cold packs keep these medicines safe for 48 hours. Swiftline delivered 14.4% of parcels after more than 48 hours, against 2.2% for Northway and 2.5% for ParcelPro.
- Each courier damaged one parcel.
- Rural deliveries take about 4 hours longer than urban and suburban ones.
- Swiftline is fastest on a typical delivery: a median of 17.9 hours, against 22.5 for Northway and 21.2 for ParcelPro.
- Parcels shipped on Mondays take longest, because of the weekend backlog.
- Overall, 17% of deliveries arrived after the time promised to the customer.
- ParcelPro only started in September, so its figures rest on 40 deliveries, against 90 for each of the others. Its single delivery over 48 hours could easily be two or three in a larger sample.
- Delivery time rises with distance (correlation 0.39 for deliveries under 48 hours).

Design guidance:
- Pick the one message the audience most needs for this decision, and make the title state it as a sentence.
- Show only the data needed for that message. Leave out series, columns and notes that do not help the decision.
- Use one strong colour for what matters and grey for context. Label lines or bars directly instead of using a legend when you can.
- Add a number label only where the number is part of the message. Do not label every bar or point.
- If a caveat changes how the chart should be read, state it briefly on the chart.
- Keep scales honest: bar charts start at zero, units are labelled, no 3-D effects and no second y-axis.

## Analyst notes
- Average order value is about the same in both versions ($413 old, $411 new).
- On mobile, conversion fell from 2.09% with the old checkout to 1.65% with the new one. On desktop it rose from 3.15% to 3.58%.
- Sessions were split evenly between the versions (50.0% old, 50.0% new), as designed.
- Tablet conversion rose from 2.35% to 2.92%, but tablets are only 3% of sessions.
- Mobile is 68% of sessions, so over the 14 days the new checkout produced 6.5% fewer orders in total (4,838 against 5,177).
- More visitors started the new checkout (+5.3% checkouts started).
- The new checkout loads faster on desktop (median 1.9 s against 2.4 s).
- A bug that hid the payment button on some phones in the new checkout was fixed on 26 September. Mobile conversion on the new checkout was 2.24% on 26 and 27 September, close to the old checkout, but two days is too short to judge.
- Conversion is highest on Saturdays in both versions.
- Both versions dipped on 20 September during a payment-provider outage.

## Analyst notes
- The January cohort is the largest (18,400 sign-ups), the New Year rush.
- Day-30 retention rose from an average of 22.3% for the January to May cohorts (old onboarding) to 31.4% for June to August (new onboarding).
- Day-1 retention is about 70% for every cohort, before and after the change.
- Lessons completed in the first 30 days rose 12% with the new onboarding.
- Only about 13% of early-2026 users are still active after 90 days.
- A TV campaign ran from June to August, the same months as the new onboarding, so part of the gain may come from different kinds of users. The September cohort, after the campaign, still reached 28.6% at day 30.
- February had the smallest cohort (9,800).
- Paid conversion within 30 days rose from 3.1% to 3.9% over the same cohorts.
- Data runs to 2 November 2026, so the September cohort is only measured to day 30 and August to day 60.
- A user counts as retained on day N if they completed a lesson on day N or later.

- Use one strong colour for what matters and grey for context. Label lines or bars directly instead of using a legend when you can.
- Add a number label only where the number is part of the message. Do not label every bar or point.
- If a caveat changes how the chart should be read, state it briefly on the chart.
- Keep scales honest: bar charts start at zero, units are labelled, no 3-D effects and no second y-axis.

## Analyst notes
- Across all 90 days the forecast was off by 1.3% on average.
- Wind speed has almost no relation to peak demand (correlation -0.02).
- The forecast under-predicts demand on very cold days. On the 7 days below −15 °C, actual peak demand was 5.3% above the forecast on average (about 47 MW).
- Weekend peaks are about 12% lower than weekday peaks.
- The share of demand from homes rises in cold weather.
- Peak demand exceeded available capacity on 4 days, 12 to 15 January, and the shortfall was covered with emergency imports.
- Imports at the daily peak averaged 22 MW.
- Unit 3 (50 MW) was out for repair from 10 to 16 January, cutting available capacity from 960 to 910 MW. With Unit 3 running, only 14 January would have exceeded capacity.
- The highest peak of the winter was 1,012 MW on 14 January.
- On mild days (above −3 °C) the forecast slightly over-predicts, by 1.8% on average.

- Add a number label only where the number is part of the message. Do not label every bar or point.
- If a caveat changes how the chart should be read, state it briefly on the chart.
- Keep scales honest: bar charts start at zero, units are labelled, no 3-D effects and no second y-axis.

The first version had the right message, but it was hard to see in ten seconds. The decisive part, a two-day red sliver, was squeezed into a 90-day series. The shortfall numbers were also hard to follow, because the "+40 MW" line steps down during the outage. This version keeps the season chart as context and adds a small panel that shows the 14 January shortfall in three cases. The bars start at zero.

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.dates as mdates

df = pd.read_csv("data.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
x = mdates.date2num(df["date"])
demand = df["actual_peak_mw"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
cap = df["available_capacity_mw"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
cap40 = cap + 40

RED = "#c62828"
GREY = "#9e9e9e"
DARK = "#424242"
MUTED = "#555555"

# Worst day and its shortfall in three cases
i_max = int(np.argmax(demand))
d_max = demand[i_max]
full_cap = cap.max()                           # 960 MW with Unit 3 running
short_actual = d_max - cap[i_max]              # Unit 3 out, no extra capacity
short_plus40 = d_max - (cap[i_max] + 40)       # Unit 3 out, +40 MW
short_plus40_full = d_max - (full_cap + 40)    # Unit 3 running, +40 MW

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
axL = fig.add_axes([0.07, 0.16, 0.56, 0.60])
axR = fig.add_axes([0.70, 0.16, 0.27, 0.60])

# ---------- Left panel: the season, for context ----------
axL.plot(x, demand, color=GREY, lw=1.4, zorder=3)
axL.plot(x, cap, drawstyle="steps-mid", color=DARK, lw=1.8, zorder=2)
axL.plot(x, cap40, drawstyle="steps-mid", color=DARK, lw=1.2, ls="--", zorder=2)

over = demand > cap
axL.fill_between(x, cap, demand, where=over, interpolate=True,
                 color=RED, alpha=0.85, lw=0, zorder=4)
axL.plot(x[i_max], d_max, "o", color=RED, ms=6, zorder=5)
axL.text(x[i_max] - 2.5, 1032, f"14 Jan, \u221229 \u00b0C: {d_max:,.0f} MW",
         ha="right", va="center", fontsize=9.5, color=RED, fontweight="bold")

axL.text(x[i_max] + 5, 918,
         "Demand above capacity on 4 days, 12\u201315 Jan\n"
         "(Unit 3, 50 MW, out for repair 10\u201316 Jan)",
         ha="left", va="top", fontsize=9, color=DARK)

# Direct line labels
axL.text(x[-1], 1003, "Capacity + 40 MW: 1,000 MW", ha="right", va="bottom",
         fontsize=9, color=DARK)
axL.text(x[-1], 963, "Available capacity: 960 MW", ha="right", va="bottom",
         fontsize=9, color=DARK)
axL.text(x[-1], 548, "Daily peak demand", ha="right", va="bottom",
         fontsize=9, color="#757575")

axL.set_xlim(x[0] - 1, x[-1] + 1)
axL.set_ylim(540, 1060)
axL.set_ylabel("MW", fontsize=10)
axL.xaxis.set_major_locator(mdates.MonthLocator())
axL.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%b %Y"))
axL.yaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:,.0f}"))
for s in ("top", "right"):
    axL.spines[s].set_visible(False)
axL.grid(axis="y", color="#e6e6e6", lw=0.8)
axL.set_axisbelow(True)
axL.tick_params(labelsize=9)
axL.set_title("Daily peak demand vs capacity, Dec 2025 \u2013 Feb 2026",
              loc="left", fontsize=10.5, color=DARK, pad=8)

# ---------- Right panel: the decision ----------
cases = [
    ("As it happened (Unit 3 out)", short_actual, GREY),
    ("With +40 MW, Unit 3 out", short_plus40, RED),
    ("With +40 MW, Unit 3 running", short_plus40_full, RED),
]
ypos = [2, 1, 0]
for (label, val, col), y in zip(cases, ypos):
    axR.barh(y, val, height=0.42, color=col, zorder=2)
    axR.text(0, y + 0.27, label, ha="left", va="bottom", fontsize=9, color=DARK)
    axR.text(val + 2.5, y, f"{val:,.0f} MW", ha="left", va="center",
             fontsize=10, fontweight="bold", color=col if col == RED else DARK)

axR.set_xlim(0, 130)

              color=DARK, pad=8)

fig.text(0.01, 0.975,

         fontsize=15, fontweight="bold", va="top", ha="left")
fig.text(0.01, 0.905,

fig.text(0.01, 0.02,
```

- **Simpler season chart.** The two shades of red fill are gone, along with the subtitle that explained them. Red now marks only the days demand went above capacity.

F1 [SECONDARY] Courier prices are within 50 cents of each other ($9.28 to $9.73 per delivery).

F3 [CRITICAL] Cold packs keep these medicines safe for 48 hours. Swiftline delivered 14.4% of parcels after more than 48 hours, against 2.2% for Northway and 2.5% for ParcelPro.
F4 [SECONDARY] Each courier damaged one parcel.
F5 [SECONDARY] Rural deliveries take about 4 hours longer than urban and suburban ones.
F6 [CRITICAL] Swiftline is fastest on a typical delivery: a median of 17.9 hours, against 22.5 for Northway and 21.2 for ParcelPro.
F7 [SECONDARY] Parcels shipped on Mondays take longest, because of the weekend backlog.
F8 [SECONDARY] Overall, 17% of deliveries arrived after the time promised to the customer.
F9 [CAVEAT] ParcelPro only started in September, so its figures rest on 40 deliveries, against 90 for each of the others. Its single delivery over 48 hours could easily be two or three in a larger sample.

- "called_out": the chart states it in text (title, subtitle, annotation or label) or draws attention to it (highlight colour, arrow, reference line or shading).
- "visible": the data behind it can be read from the chart, but nothing points to it.
- "absent": it cannot be read from the chart.

- "overload" from 1 to 5: 1 = nothing competes with the main message; 3 = some clutter; 5 = so much text, labelling, series or colour that the main message is hard to find.
- "clarity" from 1 to 5: 5 = the decision-critical message is obvious within ten seconds; 1 = the reader cannot tell what matters.
- "caveat_handling": "stated" if the chart states the CAVEAT note; "avoided" if the chart leaves out the affected data so the caveat no longer applies; "missing" if the affected data is shown without the caveat.
- "errors": a list of factual errors or misleading choices (wrong numbers, mislabelled series, bar axes not starting at zero, garbled, overlapping or unreadable text). An empty list if there are none.
- "overall" from 1 to 10: how ready the chart is to show this audience as it is.

F1 [SECONDARY] Courier prices are within 50 cents of each other ($9.28 to $9.73 per delivery).

F3 [CRITICAL] Cold packs keep these medicines safe for 48 hours. Swiftline delivered 14.4% of parcels after more than 48 hours, against 2.2% for Northway and 2.5% for ParcelPro.
F4 [SECONDARY] Each courier damaged one parcel.
F5 [SECONDARY] Rural deliveries take about 4 hours longer than urban and suburban ones.
F6 [CRITICAL] Swiftline is fastest on a typical delivery: a median of 17.9 hours, against 22.5 for Northway and 21.2 for ParcelPro.
F7 [SECONDARY] Parcels shipped on Mondays take longest, because of the weekend backlog.
F8 [SECONDARY] Overall, 17% of deliveries arrived after the time promised to the customer.
F9 [CAVEAT] ParcelPro only started in September, so its figures rest on 40 deliveries, against 90 for each of the others. Its single delivery over 48 hours could easily be two or three in a larger sample.
F10 [SECONDARY] Delivery time rises with distance (correlation 0.39 for deliveries under 48 hours).

- "absent": it cannot be read from the chart.
